Every record behind the two Cyprus pages, stored once: 1448 records from gid's memory, 1349 of them cited on a page. Each entry is the record word for word, the document it was read in and the date, and the pages that cite it. The pages link here instead of repeating the text.

How to read an entry: the type (fact, note for gid's own reading, event); the channel (chan: primary is the document itself, archive a saved copy, press a report of it, inferred gid's reading of several records); num: whether a number's method is published (sourced) or not (unsourced); cred: how far it is confirmed. Groups follow the first topic tag of each record; within a group the newest reading comes first.

  1. SumUp's Cyprus help centre (article 'Bank account compatibility', el-CY, undated, read 6 October 2026) lets a sole trader receive payouts into a personal bank account: under 'I am a sole trader' the account must be held in a euro-area country, and its holder must match the SumUp profile holder 'for personal accounts' or the registered business name 'for business bank accounts'; one account at a time. The same article says that separating personal and business money 'is necessary' for compliance with anti-money-laundering standards, linking Directive (EU) 2018/843, without making a separate account a condition.

  2. Whether a new Cyprus business must accept cards for payments by consumers turns on its main activity code. Decree K.D.P. 259/2021 under art. 30A of Law 4/1978 listed 87 codes; K.D.P. 52/2022 added taxis (49.32) and K.D.P. 248/2022 four personal-service codes (96.01, 96.03, 96.04, 96.09). The list takes in most in-store retail codes from 47.11 to 47.78 and restaurants and bars (56.10, 56.30), but not retail via mail order or internet (47.91), computer programming or IT consultancy (62) or management consultancy (70.22). A listed business that starts after the original deadline must comply within one month of starting (para. 3(δ)). cylaw's indexes to K.D.P. 372/2026 show no later amendment.

    fact · chan:primary num:derived cred:primary-confirmed claim:no-resolver · read 2026-10-06 · Official Gazette of the Republic of Cyprus, Part III(I) (cylaw copies) · doc: cylaw.org · doc2: cylaw.org

The Annex of Decree K.D.P. 259/2021 (read 6 October 2026) lists legal activities (69.10), accounting, bookkeeping, auditing and tax consultancy (69.20), architects (71.11), engineering and related technical consultancy (71.12), photography (74.20), veterinary activities (75.00), education codes such as 85.51, 85.53 and 85.59, medical and dental practice (86.21-86.23) and computer repair (95.11). No amendment after K.D.P. 248/2022 appears in cylaw's indexes to K.D.P. 372/2026.

Shopify Payments, which Shopify lists as available in Cyprus, takes a one-person business with no registration at all: its Cyprus requirements page (undated, read 6 October 2026) says to choose 'Individual / Sole Trader' if 'you haven't registered with any government agency, or you have registered but run the business as a sole trader', for one owner 'living in Cyprus', freelancers included. Such a seller gives legal name, date of birth, e-mail, phone and a Cyprus home address; no tax or VAT number is listed for this type, unlike a company. Payouts need a euro SEPA account with an IBAN from listed countries; savings, multi-currency and money-transfer-service accounts are refused.

  19. Cyprus's card-acceptance rules say nothing about the account into which takings are paid. Art. 30A of Law 4/1978, Decree K.D.P. 259/2021 with amending K.D.P. 446/2021, 52/2022 and 248/2022, and the Tax Department's Implementing Directive 20/2021 (all read 6 October 2026) require no business bank account, registered business name or company. They regulate the means: a contract with a lawfully licensed payment service provider or its agent; four-party scheme cards accepted by POS, mobile or virtual POS (credit transfer, direct debit and e-banking do not count); notices at entrance and till. The directive: the duty applies 'regardless of' amount, turnover and VAT registration.

  21. Cyprus's duty to accept cards can bind a self-employed person trading in his own name; no text names the self-employed, the reading rests on the definitions. Law 4/1978 (consolidated, read 6 October 2026) defines a 'payee' as 'the natural or legal person' that is the final recipient of the funds (Article 2(13) of Regulation (EU) 2015/751); art. 30A(1) obliges payees, in transactions with consumers, to accept cards as a decree sets by activity code, and K.D.P. 259/2021 (Annex amended by K.D.P. 446/2021, 52/2022 and 248/2022) binds payees whose main activity codes are listed. A 'consumer' acts outside his trade, business or profession, so payments by business clients fall outside the duty.

  28. ECB detailed card statistics (dataflow PCP) give the point-of-sale location of payments acquired by Cyprus-resident providers. Of 1,576 million payments worth EUR 63.8 billion in 2025 (second half provisional), 369 million and EUR 20.1 billion were initiated at points of sale in Cyprus and 1,207 million and EUR 43.7 billion abroad - 77% by number, 68% by value; of those abroad, 903 million and EUR 31.0 billion in other EEA countries, 304 million and EUR 12.7 billion outside the EEA. In 2022 the share abroad was 79% by number and 62% by value. Cyprus-licensed acquirers thus work mainly for points of sale outside the island; acquirers passported into Cyprus are not in these figures.

  35. Article 50ΣΤ of Cyprus's Law 4/1978 sets a short procedure for the card-acceptance fine (consolidated text read 5 October 2026). The officer who finds the breach reports to the Tax Commissioner within five working days, and the decision imposing the fine is issued within fifteen working days of the report. The business may object to the Commissioner within 30 days of notification and the Commissioner decides within 30 days; the decision on the objection can be taken to the Administrative Court, and a fine already paid is returned if the objection or the action succeeds. An unpaid fine is recovered as a civil debt. Implementing Directive 05/2020 (3 November 2020) restates these steps.

Mastercard Rule 7.1 (edition 2 June 2026) sorts third parties around an acquirer by 'Program Service': an Independent Sales Organization solicits merchants, processes applications and deploys terminals; a Merchant Payment Gateway sends transaction data from merchant to acquirer; a Payment Facilitator contracts with sponsored merchants as the acquirer's agent and pays them. Rule 7.6.1 requires the Merchant Agreement to be signed by the acquirer, with no separate agreement between Service Provider and merchant; if the Service Provider is a party to it, the agreement must deny it access to funds due to the merchant. Under paragraph 4 of Decree K.D.P. 259/2021 a Cyprus business meets the card-acceptance obligation with any acceptance device or method - wired or wireless POS, mobile POS, virtual POS, card-present or distance sales - but not with credit transfer, direct debit or e-banking, which the decree says are not a card-acceptance terminal. It must accept cards of four-party schemes 'such as VISA, MASTER CARD, MAESTRO, UNION PAY', acceptance of three-party scheme cards is not obligatory, and it must contract only with lawfully licensed payment service providers under Law 31(I)/2018 or their agents; paragraph 6 requires clear notice of card acceptance at the shop entrance and at the till.

Mastercard's Site Data Protection programme (Security Rules and Procedures - Merchant Edition, 4 August 2026, section 2.2.2) sets how a merchant validates PCI DSS compliance: Level 1 (more than six million combined Mastercard and Maestro transactions a year, or designated by Mastercard) - annual assessment with a Report on Compliance; Level 2 (more than one million up to six million) - annual SAQ, with a QSA or ISA for SAQ A, A-EP or D; Level 3 (more than 20,000 up to one million e-commerce transactions) - annual SAQ; all other merchants are Level 4 - compliance required, SAQ optional. A Cyprus business obliged to accept cards escapes the fine where it objectively cannot obtain a terminal (Article 50ΣΤ(8) of the Assessment and Collection of Taxes Law 4/1978, consolidated text read 4 October 2026): the fine is not imposed if at the inspection it shows a document certifying that a licensed payment service provider rejected its application for a terminal, or if it applied before the deadline and the terminal was not supplied for reasons attributable to the credit institution, certified in writing. Under Decree K.D.P. 259/2021, paragraph 3(δ), a business that starts a listed activity after the initial deadline has one month from the start or the change to comply.

  112. Cyprus tax law says with whom a merchant may contract for card acceptance. Art. 30A(2) of Law 4/1978 (in force since 20 August 2020): to accept card payment instruments, payees contract with lawfully licensed payment service providers within the meaning of the Payment Services Law 31(I)/2018; the proviso forbids payees, for card acceptance and for collection on behalf of a third party generally, to contract with entities that are not lawfully licensed payment service providers or their agents, unless legislation expressly provides otherwise. Decree K.D.P. 259/2021 repeats the rule, and breaches of the decree are finable under art. 50ΣΤ. The text does not mention payment facilitators.

Visa classifies as a Marketplace only an entity that: brings cardholders and retailers together on a website or app; shows its brand more prominently than the retailers' and in the app name or URL; handles payments and receives settlement for the retailers; is financially liable for disputes and resolves them by a binding decision or a money-back guarantee it funds; and lets no retailer outside its jurisdiction exceed both USD 10 million in annual Visa volume through it and 10% of its annual Visa volume (5.3.4.1, ID# 0030069, edition 18 April 2026). Surcharging by merchants in Cyprus, Payment Services Law 31(I)/2018 (consolidated text read 4 October 2026): art. 62(5) — a payee may not request charges for the use of a specific payment instrument; art. 62(4) — a charge is never allowed for instruments whose interchange fees are capped under Chapter II of Regulation (EU) 2015/751 or for payments under Regulation (EU) No 260/2012; art. 60(1) — where a payee charges or offers a discount for a given instrument it must tell the payer before the payment is initiated. Under art. 99(1A) the Consumer Protection Service, not the Central Bank, is the competent authority for payees' compliance with arts 60 and 62.

  122. JCC's published terms (v2.10) say JCC 'will create a Collateral' at signing if, in its sole judgment, the merchant's activities might damage its interests. It consists of either or both of: a rolling reserve — a percentage of each day's gross sales (less MSC) retained for a period, both set in the individual agreement — and a bank guarantee for a percentage of anticipated gross purchases. JCC may also withhold or delay payments to build a chargeback reserve or collateral (§6.2, §7.5), and after termination keeps the collateral for one year from the last transaction, or indefinitely after material breach. Where the law requires, withheld amounts are safeguarded in segregated client accounts.

Mastercard mandates MATCH Pro for all acquirers with merchant activity, unless excused by Mastercard or prohibited by law (Security Rules and Procedures - Merchant Edition, 4 August 2026, sections 11.3, 7.1.1). An acquirer must check MATCH Pro before signing a merchant or enabling acceptance (section 11.6) and, when either side acts to terminate while a listed reason-code condition is believed to exist, must add the merchant within five calendar days (11.5). Records stay five years and are then purged automatically (11.10). A listing does not bar onboarding (11.2), and MATCH Pro may not be used or threatened as a collection tool for minor discretionary merchant activity (11.4, item 8).

Visa requires an acquirer to hold a Merchant Agreement with each merchant, and a payment facilitator to hold one with each sponsored merchant; the agreement must oblige the merchant to follow applicable law and the Visa Rules, not to submit illegal transactions, and must reserve Visa's right to limit or terminate it (Visa Core Rules section 1.5.2.1, ID# 0003356, edition 18 April 2026, last updated Oct 2025). The acquirer or facilitator may accept transactions only from an entity with which it has a valid Merchant Agreement.

Whoever keeps or uses business premises in a Cyprus municipality - an office, a shop or a cafe - is charged a yearly professional or trade fee under s. 56(5) of the Municipalities Law 52(I)/2022, within the Fifth Schedule's ceilings: self-employed craftsmen EUR 50; professionals, traders and businessmen working as individuals EUR 200; private companies with up to 5 employees EUR 150, 6-15 EUR 250, 16-30 EUR 350, over 30 EUR 500; partnerships the same; insurance, shipping, airline, banking, financing and portfolio companies and public companies EUR 1,000; others EUR 300. Premises opened in the second half-year pay half; rises are capped at 10% a year; the council may exempt kinds of business.

Fire safety of Cyprus buildings is designed to Annex IV ('Fire Protection Regulation') of the Streets and Buildings Regulations, as replaced by decree K.D.P. 400/2020 (Gazette 27 August 2020) for developments without a planning or building permit or application by 31 August 2020; the designer applies it, and the Fire Service may set other conditions when consulted (paras 1.3, 1.9). Alterations, additions or repairs to an existing licensed building must at least meet Chapter 7 (emergency evacuation) and use suitable products (Chapter 9) (para. 1.10). Shops need emergency lighting on escape routes, except ground-floor shops under 100 m2 of sales area with exits within 15 m (Table 33).

  7. A Cyprus cafe selling alcohol needs a retail licence under the Sale of Intoxicating Liquors Law, Cap. 144, from the municipal council, or the District Officer outside municipalities (s. 2). Its Annex sets the yearly fee for a general retail licence for consumption on or off the premises at CY£80 inside a municipality, CY£50 elsewhere, and CY£200 where entertainment by artists with music or songs is offered (€136.68, €85.43, €341.72 in the portal's table); half is due for a licence granted after 13 September (s. 13(1)). A licence expires on the 12 March following issue (s. 11); an application not answered within two months of complete papers, extendable once, is deemed granted (s. 11A).

Yearly ceilings under the Municipalities Law 52(I)/2022 (Schedules read 6 October 2026), as we map the reader's cases (the council sets the category): a person trading in his own name from a shop, café or one-person office most plausibly fits the Fifth Schedule's 'traders ... and businessmen, working as individuals', up to €200 (a self-employed craftsman €50; unlisted €300), and owes no s. 56(6) fee, which falls on legal persons only. A Cyprus trader selling goods to consumers must show the selling price and the unit price (per kg, litre, metre, m2 or m3, or per item) including VAT and all taxes, in euro, clearly and legibly, on the goods, the packaging or the shelf; where goods in a shop are not within the customer's reach a price list must be displayed (ss. 42, 44 of the Consumer Protection Law 112(I)/2021). Advertisements that state a price give the unit price too (s. 43). Any announced price reduction must state the earlier price - the lowest in the 30 days before the reduction, except for goods that perish or expire quickly or have been on the market under 30 days (s. 45(2)). Read 6 October 2026.

Under Cyprus's Catering Establishments (Sound Emission Licences) Law 50(I)/2016 (as amended to 2021; read 6 Oct 2026), a catering establishment sited where it causes or may cause noise nuisance to nearby homes may not emit sound beyond its plot unless its owner first obtains a sound emission licence from the municipality, or the District Officer outside municipalities, unless a ministerial decree names another body (ss. 2, 3(1)). Cyprus's General Development Order 2024 (K.D.P. 181/2024, Gazette 10 May 2024) lets a building used for a purpose in use classes I-VIII of its Second Annex be used for another purpose of the same class without planning permission (para. 5(1)), unless a permit condition bars it (para. 5(3)). A business importing goods from outside the EU registers with customs (EORI): under art. 9(1) of the Union Customs Code, Regulation (EU) No 952/2013, economic operators established in the EU customs territory 'shall register with the customs authorities responsible for the place where they are established'. Turning a Cyprus shop or office into a cafe engages building and planning law: s. 3(1)(ε) of Cap. 96 (Streets and Buildings Regulation Law) forbids anyone to change, or permit or tolerate a change of, the approved use of a building without a permit obtained beforehand from the competent authority - now the district EOA's Director of Development Licensing (s. 2). The paragraph stands apart from building works (para. (β)), so on its wording it applies even where no works are done. Planning permission is needed too: only changes within a use class are free of it, and shop (class I), office (II) and cafe (III) are different classes (General Development Order 2024, para. 5, Second Schedule).

A restaurant, taverna, cafeteria, bar or similar place serving food or drink for payment in Cyprus may not operate without a licence under the Catering Establishments Law 29/1985 (s. 6(1)), issued by the Deputy Ministry of Tourism (Law 123(I)/2018). Section 2 excludes traditional coffee-shops ('καφενεία'), take-away-only shops, certain canteens, and shops with a service area under 8 m² serving no alcohol. The licence needs a sanitary certificate and the fee (s. 6(3)) and, since Law 170(I)/2020, expires every three years. Staff who handle unpacked food in a Cyprus food business need a Health Certificate for Food Handlers from a Chief Medical Officer of the Ministry of Health: per the business portal (updated 2 May 2024) there is no application form; a stool sample is tested for salmonella and parasites at the person's own cost, then the officer issues the certificate the same day for €22 plus a registration fee; it is valid twelve months.   120. A licensed catering establishment in Cyprus must have a manager who meets statutory conditions, and the owner may fill the post only if he meets them (Law 29/1985, s. 16; read 5 Oct 2026). The manager must be a graduate of a recognised hotel or tourism school with knowledge of food and drink, or hold a secondary-school leaving certificate and one year's catering experience, or have at least three years' experience judged satisfactory by the licensing authority; and must be of good character, shown by a Chief of Police certificate of no conviction for listed offences. For class A and B establishments only the school route counts. The Law sets no nationality condition for the manager.

Law 73(I)/2009 has a general route for sanctions under EU acts assigned to CySEC by notification: article 37(1A) (consolidated text on cylaw.org, read 5 October 2026) obliges the Commission to impose the administrative sanctions and measures laid down in European Union acts for whose application it is designated competent authority 'either under those acts or by notification of the Minister'; article 37(1) sets the general fine at up to EUR 350,000, EUR 700,000 on repetition. Read with K.D.P. 310/2024 this would cover MiCA without a dedicated law - an inference, not a CySEC statement. The provision speaks of the Commission only; the Central Bank's corresponding power was not checked.

  122. Inside a municipality a café needs municipal licences beside the tourism licence. Under the Municipalities Law 52(I)/2022, premises over 50 m² used as a restaurant, taverna, snack bar, cafeteria or pizzeria need a prior municipal licence under s. 55(1)(γ), for up to three years, on a building permit and engineer's, electrical, fire and municipal-health certificates; s. 56(1), the licence for any business premises, excepts those cases and so covers smaller ones. Section 44(1) adds sound-emission and alcohol licences; under Cap. 144, s. 11, an alcohol licence expires on 12 March. The business portal, still citing the 1985 Law, gives four months for the premises decision, two for alcohol.

Derived from the rates in force on 6 October 2026, for company profit of tax year 2026 or later paid out in full as a dividend to a Cyprus tax-resident individual: corporate tax 15%, then on the remaining 85% a 5% special defence contribution if the shareholder is also domiciled in Cyprus, and 2.65% GeSY on the dividend, which has no domicile test - in all 15% + 85% x 7.65% = 21.5025% of the profit, or 15% + 85% x 2.65% = 17.2525% for a non-domiciled resident. A sole trader's profit instead bears the personal scale (0% up to €22,000, 35% above €72,000), social insurance at the applied 16.6% between his category minimum and the ceiling, 4% GeSY and, from 6 April 2026, a 0.5% training levy.

  6. A Cyprus partnership is taxed through its partners, not as an entity. Under s. 7 of the Assessment and Collection of Taxes Law 4/1978 (consolidated text read 6 October 2026), where a business or profession is carried on jointly by two or more persons, each partner's taxable income from the partnership is his share of its income for the tax year, entered in his own return; and a partner who must register in the tax register files each year a return of the partnership's income naming the other partners and each one's share. The Income Tax Law's definition of 'company', which the 15% corporate rate applies to, excludes a partnership (Law 118(I)/2002, s. 2).

  8. Losses are used differently by rung in Cyprus. Under s. 13(1) of the Income Tax Law 118(I)/2002 (consolidated text read 6 October 2026) a loss not wholly set off against the same person's other income of that tax year is carried forward - on this wording a sole trader's business loss first reduces his other income of the year. For a person obliged to keep books, have accounts audited and file a return, carry-forward ends seven years after the loss year (five before 1 January 2026). A company's current-year loss may be surrendered within a 75% group to a Cyprus-resident company (s. 13(4)-(8)); in a merger or other reorganisation, accumulated losses pass to the receiving company (ss. 27, 29A).

  11. Dissolving a Cyprus company brings the transitional deemed-dividend charge forward. Under art. 3Γ(1)(β) of Law 117(I)/2002 (as replaced by Law 245(I)/2025), on dissolution all profits of the last five years, to the extent earned in tax years up to 2025 and not distributed or already deemed distributed, are deemed distributed, with 17% on the part attributable to individuals resident and domiciled in Cyprus; under the proviso to art. 4(5), once the company passes a resolution for voluntary dissolution or liquidation, the declaration and payment are due within one month of it.

  12. Since 1 January 2026 officers of a Cyprus company who bear criminal liability for its unpaid taxes are also civilly liable. Under s. 51A(3) of the Assessment and Collection of Taxes Law 4/1978, when a legal person fails or delays paying tax it withheld (income tax, defence contribution, the 2011-2013 special contribution), its executive director, board members and officers with financial-management duties also bear criminal liability; for other taxes, only if shown to have taken part fraudulently. New s. 51A(3A), added by Law 243(I)/2025 (in force 1 January 2026), makes such a person liable jointly or severally with the legal person in any civil proceedings. Read 6 October 2026.

Cyprus lengthened the carry-forward of tax losses from five to seven years: art. 8(α) of the Income Tax (Amendment) (No. 4) Law 244(I)/2025 (Gazette No. 5070, 31 December 2025) replaced 'five' with 'seven' in the first proviso to s. 13(1) of Law 118(I)/2002, in force from 1 January 2026 (art. 25). Art. 8(β) makes group relief apply only after the claimant company has set off its own losses brought forward. The government's tax-reform page for businesses (modified 10 July 2026, read 6 October 2026) lists the 'extension of the loss carry-forward period to seven years'. Art. 8 says nothing on losses of years before 2026.

  21. An employer in Cyprus files a monthly return of income tax and contributions withheld from pay (PAYE) through Tax For All by the end of the month after the month of withholding. For a company first paying wages for November 2026 the Department's calendar gives 31 December 2026 (November), 31 January 2027 (December) and 31 March 2027 for the annual PAYE return for 2026.

  23. CRS self-certification at account opening has a statutory basis in Cyprus beside the ministerial decrees. Annex I, Section IV.A of the Administrative Cooperation in the Field of Taxation Law 205(I)/2012, added by Law 60(I)/2016 (Official Gazette no. 4564, 25 April 2016; transposes Directive 2014/107/EU), requires a Reporting Cyprus Financial Institution, on opening a new individual account, to obtain a self-certification that lets it determine the holder's tax residence(s) and to confirm that it is reasonable in light of the information collected at opening, including AML/KYC documentation.   26. Cyprus enforces card acceptance by inspection, not by a technical link. Article 32A of Law 4/1978, inserted by Law 243(I)/2025, lets the Tax Commissioner seal a business for up to ten days, after three notices, where it owes more than EUR 20,000, obstructs an audit, 'did not issue the invoices or receipts' the Law requires, or misses a set number of returns (two tax, twelve withholding or three VAT returns, counted from 1 January 2027); refusing cards is not a ground and stays under the fine of Article 50ΣΤ. The Cyprus Mail (20 July 2026), citing Tax Commissioner Sotiris Markides, reported inspections of whether businesses issue lawful receipts 'and allow customers to pay by card'.

Dates of the bookkeeping duties in art. 30 of Cyprus's Law 4/1978, per Tax Department Circular 2015/21 (26 November 2015): Law 135(I)/2005, in force 1 January 2006, brought the general duty to keep books and prepare accounts, the Commissioner's power of on-site audit and the period within which he may audit; Law 136(I)/2010, in force 1 July 2011, added subsections (4)-(7): inspection of business premises during working hours, books updated by the end of the fourth month after the month of the transactions, invoices issued within 30 days of the transaction, and a yearly stock count. In 2015 books were kept at least six years from the end of the tax year, wording replaced by Law 243(I)/2025.

First direct-tax dates of a Cyprus company incorporated in October 2026 (Law 4/1978 as amended from 1 January 2026): notice for the Tax Register within 60 days of incorporation - 30 November 2026 if incorporated on 1 October, 30 December if on 31 October (s. 5A(2)); its own estimate of 2026 chargeable income by 31 December 2026 (s. 24, third proviso), the provisional tax paid in one instalment by that day (s. 38(1)(γ), proviso). On 5 Oct 2026 the Tax Department's calendar shows an undated 'an extension will be given' in its 31 December 2026 provisional-tax row, but the row is titled 'for 2025' and may be a leftover. Sections 24-26 do not address a company expecting no chargeable income.

  30. Cyprus's first-employment tax exemptions need no application or approval. The first income tax return of a Cyprus company incorporated in October 2026 is for tax year 2026 and is due on 31 January 2028: s. 5(1A) of Law 4/1978 gives a person whose accounts must be audited or reviewed until 31 January of the second year after the tax year, and every company files whether or not it has income. Under the last proviso to s. 38(1)(α), for tax year 2026 onwards, the balance of tax falls due on the same 31 January 2028 - no longer on 1 August of the year after the tax year, as for tax years 2020-2025. Both dates are statutory and the return date may be extended by decree of the Council of Ministers.

Form T.D.59 for tax year 2026, 'Declaration for claiming tax deductions', is where a Cyprus employee claims a first-employment exemption in payroll: Part B, line 2, 'deduction for first employment'. Its note 7 offers three options - 20% of remuneration up to €8,550; 50% where the salary exceeds €100,000 (interpretative circular 2017/4); 50% where it exceeds €55,000 'according to circulars 2022/10 and 2024/04'. The employee's social insurance number is a mandatory field. As read on 5 October 2026 no line or note of the form names the 25% relief of art. 8(21B), although the Tax Department's FAQ of 6 August 2026 says that relief too is given without an application.

  42. A founder already living in Cyprus when his first employment there starts may fail the residence test of the 50% exemption. Per Tax Department Circular 4/2024 (8 July 2024), paras 13-14, the 15 consecutive years of non-residence are the tax years before the year in which the first employment in Cyprus starts; that year itself is not counted, whether or not the person was resident in it. Its example: a start in 2023 requires non-residence in every year from 2008 to 2022. One earlier year of Cyprus tax residence breaks the chain. The 20% exemption instead requires three consecutive years of employment outside Cyprus for a non-resident employer immediately before (Circular 10/2022, part II).

  46. Non-domicile status in Cyprus is claimed by a declaration the tax office records; the form has no approval step. The Tax Department's page (updated 11 September 2026) calls it a 'request for exemption' made on form T.D.38 (2016), with questionnaires T.D.38ΕρΑ (domicile of origin) and T.D.38ΕρΒ (domicile of choice), sent to the District Tax Office. Per the form, a tax-resident individual files it with the returns section of the office holding his file 'in the first year of acquiring income from dividends / interest / rent' in which he considers himself exempt; he declares under 17 years' residence in the last 20, and one without a Cyprus domicile of origin ticks box 2 and attaches T.D.38ΕρΑ.

  47. Cyprus law gives an individual no day-count deadline for tax registration. Section 5A(1A) of the Assessment and Collection of Taxes Law 4/1978, inserted by art. 5 of Law 243(I)/2025 (in force 1 January 2026), obliges an individual to give notice for registration and obtain a TIN where he is resident in Cyprus and has reached the age of 25, or has income falling under art. 5 of the Income Tax Law; unlike s. 5A(2) for companies (60 days) it states no period. A proviso lets a person with no such income in tax years 2026 and 2027, not yet registered, give the notice until 31 December 2027. A founder who draws a salary has such income and is outside the proviso.

  53. Cyprus's 50% exemption is anchored to the first employment in Cyprus, not to the founder's own company. Art. 8(23A) proviso (iv) of Law 118(I)/2002: 'first employment' starts when a person, after 15 consecutive tax years without any salaried services in Cyprus, begins such services for a resident or non-resident employer. Tax Department Circular 4/2024 (8 July 2024), para 10: whoever performed salaried services in Cyprus, of any duration, in the 15 tax years before is not eligible; para 11: services count when performed with physical presence in Cyprus. The Department's FAQ (updated 6 August 2026) adds that changing employer does not affect eligibility. Art. 8(21A) uses the same definition.

  55. Cyprus has a third relief beside the 20% and 50% exemptions. Law 17(I)/2026 (Gazette 6 March 2026, deemed in force 1 January 2025) added art. 8(21B) to Income Tax Law 118(I)/2002: 25% of pay from employment in Cyprus, or of an individual's business profits there, is exempt up to €25,000 a year, in the start year and the six following, each year the income exceeds €30,000. It reaches only a person who starts in 2025-2030, was not resident in the seven tax years before the start year but was resident in an earlier year, and worked full time abroad for a non-resident employer for 84 months, or 36 of the last 84 with a recognised degree. It excludes art. 8(21A) and is excluded by art. 8(23A).

  58. Cyprus's non-domicile regime survived the 2026 reform. Among individuals, SDC is charged only on those who are both tax resident and domiciled in Cyprus; an individual tax resident for at least 17 of the last 20 years before the tax year is deemed domiciled. New art. 3Δ of SDC Law 117(I)/2002 (added by Law 245(I)/2025, in force 1 January 2026) lets a person without a Cyprus domicile of origin who has become deemed-domiciled opt, irrevocably, for a flat SDC of €50,000 a year, paid as a single €250,000 instalment per five-year period, for up to two periods; the application is due by 30 June of the first year of the period and must be accepted by the Tax Commissioner.

Provisional tax in Cyprus: a person with income other than emoluments submits its own estimate of the year's chargeable income before 31 July of the tax year (art. 24 of Law 4/1978) and pays in two instalments — the Tax Department's deadline calendar for 2026 lists 31 July and 31 December. The estimate can be revised until 31 December. If the provisional chargeable income is below three quarters of the final figure, an additional tax of one tenth of the difference between final tax and provisional tax is due (art. 26(1)). A company formed after 30 June files its estimate by 31 December (proviso added by Law 243(I)/2025).

  105. Dividends paid by a Cyprus company to non-residents after the 2026 reform bear no general withholding. Among recipients abroad, art. 3(1)(δ) of SDC Law 117(I)/2002 (as replaced by Law 245(I)/2025, in force 1 January 2026) reaches only a non-resident company, or a permanent establishment kept there, resident or registered in a low-tax jurisdiction (5%) or in an EU-listed non-cooperative jurisdiction (17%; 17% if both), and only where payer and recipient are linked by more than 50% of votes, capital or profit rights; listed securities are excepted if the payer cannot reasonably know. The 17% charge dates from Law 195(I)/2021 (in force 31 December 2022), the low-tax limb from Law 48(I)/2025.

  107. Outline, not a computation: paying a Cyprus director a salary versus a dividend after 1 January 2026. Salary: deductible against the 15% corporate tax; taxed in the director's hands on the 0-35% scale (first €22,000 at 0%); social insurance 8.8% employee plus 8.8% employer up to the insurable ceiling; GeSY 2.65% plus 2.90%; employer-only funds 1.2%, 0.5% and 2% (the 2% Social Cohesion Fund has no earnings ceiling). Dividend: paid out of profit after 15% corporate tax; SDC 5% - or 17% if paid by 31/12/2031 by a Cyprus-resident company out of profits of years up to 2025 - and only if the recipient is resident and domiciled; GeSY 2.65% on the dividend, with all GeSY-liable income capped at €180,000 a year; no social insurance.

  9. Cyprus's Aliens and Immigration Regulations 1972-2013 use two officer titles. A lower-case 'λειτουργός μεταναστεύσεως' (immigration officer) issues transit and visitor permits (regs 10(1), 14(1)) and, on the Τμηματάρχης's written approval, employment permits (11(1)). The 'Τμηματάρχης', defined in reg. 2 as the Immigration Officer in the Immigration Service, decides independent-profession permits (12(6)) and pupil's permits (13(1)), extends permitted stays (9(6)), grants re-entry permits (9(7)) and gives a visitor prior written permission to work or do business (14(3)); without it, taking a job ends the visitor's permit and doing business may get it revoked (14(4)).

Law 4(I)/2025 (Gazette No. 5026, 14.2.2025) deletes the term, defines the Department as the Migration Department of Law 23(I)/2024 (s. 2) and lets the Council of Ministers or Deputy Minister delegate powers to the Director or staff (s. 3). Quality criteria of Cyprus's investor-permit policy (4th revision, read 6 Oct 2026): applicant and spouse file clean criminal record certificates from their country of origin and their country of residence if different, and must not threaten public order or security; applicant and dependants file a health insurance certificate covering inpatient and outpatient care. For categories B-D, or where the new home has too few bedrooms for the family, evidence of accommodation in Cyprus is required (title, sale contract with proof of payment, or a lease). Applicant and spouse also sign a statement that they will take no employment except as directors of the company they invested in.

The four €300,000 investments of Cyprus's investor-permit policy (4th revision, in force 2 May 2023; read 6 Oct 2026): (A) a house or flat bought new from a development company, €300,000 plus VAT, up to two units, resales only if the contract was filed with the Land Registry before 7 May 2013; (B) other real estate - offices, shops, hotels - which may be a resale; (C) €300,000 into the share capital of a new or existing Cyprus company based and operating in Cyprus, with proven physical presence and at least five employees (proved by Social Insurance records); (D) €300,000 in units of a Cyprus AIF, AIFLNP or RAIF whose investments are held in Cyprus, with CySEC's confirmation of the fund.

How an EU citizen going self-employed in Cyprus meets the Migration Department, read together (6 October 2026): the registration certificate may not be made a condition for exercising a right that can be proved by other means (Law 7(I)/2007 art. 23(1)), yet he must apply for it within four months of arrival (art. 10(1)); Social Insurance registration is due at the latest on the day the work starts, with an ID card or passport; the Department's MEU1 list then asks for four months of paid contributions (or, if insured in another EU state, form A1 and health insurance), while the Law asks only 'proof of self-employment' (art. 10(4)(α)).   25. Cyprus's investment citizenship programme and the Regulation 6(2) investor permit were different instruments that met at one point. The programme naturalised investors 'by exception' under s. 111A(2) of the Civil Registry Laws. The 6(2) permit alone gives residence, not citizenship.

Reading the Cyprus texts together (6 Oct 2026), the Regulation 6(2) investor permit is a status of a person - permanent residence for investor and family for €300,000 invested and €50,000 income, with no employment except as director of the company invested in (or, if not investing in shares, unpaid director of Cyprus companies). A 'company of foreign interests' is a status of a company - registered by the Business Facilitation Unit on a €200,000 initial investment - that may employ third-country nationals on temporary residence and employment permits, directors among the staff categories. The investor route rests on this power and a published policy, not a law: the 'Criteria for granting an Immigration Permit within the scope of the expedited procedure', 4th revision, in force 2 May 2023, issued by the Minister of Interior 'having notified the Council of Ministers'. It requires €300,000 invested (new dwelling, other real estate, shares of a Cyprus company with five staff, or fund units) and €50,000 annual income. From 3 March 2026 the 3rd revision (24 March 2021) is closed to new filings.

  54. Immigration applications in Cyprus are handled by the Migration Department of the Deputy Ministry of Migration and International Protection. Law 23(I)/2024 moved the Civil Registry and Migration Department out of the Ministry of Interior and renamed it Migration Department (art. 5(4)(α)), leaving civil registry, marriage and citizenship matters with that Ministry; the Deputy Ministry 'was established on 17/6/24'. Until the sector laws are amended, references to the Minister of Interior are read as the Deputy Minister, except powers to issue decrees (art. 18(1)(β)) - hence the 2025 Blue Card fees decree is signed by the Minister of Interior. The Department's site is now gov.cy/mip-md.

  58. For a citizen of another EU or EEA state the registration certificate is a duty backed by a fine, not a legal precondition for economic activity in Cyprus. Art. 23(1) of Law 7(I)/2007 provides that possession of the registration certificate or permanent residence certificate may 'in no case' be imposed as a precondition for exercising a right or completing an administrative formality where entitlement can be attested by any other means of proof; being employed or self-employed is itself a ground of residence (art. 9(1)(α)). The Migration Department's MEU1 page (read 5 Oct 2026) says Union citizens 'enjoy free access to employment, including employed or self-employed activity'.

  59. Capital thresholds for the self-employment categories of the Cyprus immigration permit, in two texts. The consolidated Aliens and Immigration Regulations (to 2013; euro amounts by notice K.D.P. 312/2007) require freely disposable capital of €341,720 for Category A (agriculture) and B (mining) and €256,290 for C (trade or business), 'or such lesser sum as the Committee may decide'. The Migration Department's page (5 Oct 2026) gives 'approximately' €430,000 (CY£250,000) for A, €350,000 (CY£200,000) for B and €260,000 (CY£150,000) for C. At CY£0.585274 per euro the Regulation's sums equal CY£200,000 and CY£150,000, so the texts differ only for A. C also requires any licence the business needs.

For a third-country national the Cyprus Aliens and Immigration Regulations treat running one's own business as 'exercise of an independent profession', needing a permit (regs 9(1)(γ), 12): any activity exercised individually or as a company under the Companies Law or the partnerships law, without dependence on an employer (12(1)). Swiss citizens' free movement in Cyprus rests on a treaty, not on the text of Law 7(I)/2007: by Article 1 of the Protocol to the EC-Switzerland Agreement on the free movement of persons (OJ L 89, 28.3.2006, p. 30) the ten states that joined the EU in 2004, Cyprus among them, 'become Contracting Parties to the Agreement'. Both acts resolve in CELLAR on 5 Oct 2026 (the brackets of the CELEX number must be percent-encoded). No Cyprus law or decision applying the Law's registration procedure to Swiss citizens was found in the Law or on the Migration Department's pages; only the Department's MEU1 page says the procedure covers them.

  64. The Cyprus Digital Nomad Visa is a residence permit, not a work permit, under Council of Ministers decisions of 15 October 2021 (ceiling 100) and 3 March 2022 (ceiling 500). The ceiling was exhausted by early 2024; on 26 March 2025 applications were announced as accepted, and the page (read 5 Oct 2026) says the maximum 'remains at 500'. Regulation 12(10) of the Cyprus Aliens and Immigration Regulations bars the in-country route to the independent-profession permit: the holder of a pupil's, student's, visitor's or employment permit or of any other special permit may not, during its validity or after its expiry while remaining in the Republic, apply for it. Under 12(2) an alien 'who wishes to enter the Republic' applies through the consular authority of his country of residence or, where there is none, to the Immigration Officer (the Regulations' 'Τμηματάρχης'); under 12(11) a holder of that permit may not seek an employment permit unless he has an immigration permit. Long-term residents and EU citizens' family members have self-employment by Law, outside this permit.

Reading the Cyprus texts together for a third-country founder (5 Oct 2026): no approval to hold shares or to be entered as a director was found in the Companies Law or the immigration texts read. What is regulated is activity. Employment needs a permit naming the employer. Running a business needs a status with free access to work (long-term resident, family member of a Cypriot or EU citizen), a Startup Visa, an immigration permit in a self-employment category, or a Regulation 12 permit, which holders of visitor, student or employment permits may not apply for while in Cyprus. Which company may register as a 'company of foreign interests' in Cyprus, per the Business Facilitation Unit's page as of 5 Oct 2026: a business (e.g. a local company, HE, or an overseas company's branch, AE) meeting one of nine criteria, the first being majority ownership by third-country nationals ('50% plus'). A third-country national who is a family member of a citizen of another EU or EEA state residing in Cyprus - spouse, descendant under 21 or dependent, dependent ascendant (Law 7(I)/2007, art. 2) - may work without a work permit: under art. 21 family members of a Union citizen, irrespective of nationality, with a right of residence or permanent residence may take up employed or self-employed activity, and art. 22(1) gives them equal treatment with Cypriot citizens. A third-country national holding a visitor's permit in Cyprus (the temporary residence permit colloquially called the 'pink slip', a name absent from the Department's pages read 5 Oct 2026) is barred from economic activity by Regulation 14 of the Aliens and Immigration Regulations: the permit is issued for holidays, touring or exploring the possibility of settling (14(1)), and its holder must not seek or accept employment, paid or unpaid, or engage in or carry on any business, trade or profession in the Republic without the prior written permission of the Immigration Officer, the Regulations' 'Τμηματάρχης' (14(3)). If, without that prior permission, the holder accepts employment, the permit ceases at once and is deemed cancelled; if he engages in or carries on a business, the Immigration Officer may revoke it at once (14(4)).

  79. A family member of an EU Blue Card holder in Cyprus may run a business, which the card holder may not. Art. 18ΤΣΤ(6) of the Aliens and Immigration Law (Cap. 105, as replaced by Law 111(I)/2024) gives family members access to any employment 'as well as to self-employment' under Cyprus law, subject only to the public-authority restrictions of art. 18ΤΓ(5), and art. 18ΤΣΤ(5) bars any waiting period; the Migration Department's page (read 5 Oct 2026) puts it as 'free access to the labour market, including self-employment'. The holder's own access under art. 18ΤΓ(1) is to highly qualified employment only; the article as consolidated on CyLaw has no provision for self-employed activity alongside.

Long-term resident status gives a third-country national in Cyprus equal treatment with citizens in access to employment and self-employed activity, except activities involving public authority or reserved by law to Cypriot or EU citizens (Cap. 105, art. 18ΙΖ(1)(α)). The Immigration Control Committee grants it after five years of legal, continuous residence (art. 18Η(1)) subject to stable resources, health insurance and Greek at level A2 (art. 18Θ(1)); students and holders of a formally limited permit are excluded (art. 18Ζ(2)). As of 5 Oct 2026 form MLT3 is filed only at the Migration Department in Nicosia by appointment; fee €30; examination 6 to 12 months; first permit five years.

  88. A citizen of another EU or EEA state who has resided legally in Cyprus for a continuous period of five years has the right of permanent residence (Law 7(I)/2007, art. 14(1)); continuity is not affected by absences of up to six months a year in total (art. 14(3)) and the right is lost only by absence exceeding two consecutive years (art. 14(4)). A permanent residence certificate is issued on application for a €20 fee (art. 17(1)). As of 5 Oct 2026 the form is MEU3 (EU citizens' file MEU3B-EUROPEAN_20260309) and the Department's list asks for the MEU1 certificate, monthly Social Insurance contribution statements and tax returns for the last five years, and five years of utility bills.

  89. Under Law 7(I)/2007 a citizen of another EU or EEA state may stay in Cyprus for up to three months with no condition other than a valid identity card or passport (art. 8(1)). Beyond three months the right of residence exists if he or she is an employed or self-employed worker in the Republic, or has sufficient resources and comprehensive sickness insurance cover in the Republic, or is enrolled as a student with such insurance and a declaration of sufficient resources, or is a family member accompanying or joining such a citizen (art. 9(1)(α)-(δ)). The authority may not fix an amount that it regards as sufficient resources and must take the person's own situation into account (art. 10(5)).

The CyLaw consolidated text of the Cyprus Aliens and Immigration Law (Cap. 105) is one amendment behind on 5 Oct 2026: its amendment history ends at Law 149(I)/2024, while Law 4(I)/2025 (Official Gazette No. 5026 of 14 February 2025) amends 49 of its sections and repeals Annex III. Most changes replace 'Minister' or 'Minister of Interior' with the Deputy Minister of Migration and International Protection or the Council of Ministers; the power to fix single-permit fees by decree (art. 18ΥΕ(1Α)) passes from the Minister of Interior to the Council of Ministers. What a holder of the Cyprus investor immigration permit (Regulation 6(2) policy, 4th revision in force 2 May 2023) may do in a company: applicant and spouse confirm that they do not intend to undertake any form of employment in the Republic, 'with the exception of their employment as Directors in a Company in which they have chosen to invest under this policy' (para 3.3). Where the investment is not in a company's share capital they 'are permitted to be shareholders in companies registered in Cyprus', dividends are no obstacle, and in such companies they 'may also hold the position of an unpaid Director' (para 3.4).   26. How the three large Cyprus banks use Law 31(I)/2018 against a company that is not a micro-enterprise (terms published on 4 October 2026). Notice of changes to terms and fees: Bank of Cyprus none; Eurobank none (ex-Hellenic terms) or two months (ex-Eurobank Cyprus terms); Alpha two months, interest rates excepted. Termination by the bank: Bank of Cyprus immediate; Eurobank 'without notice'; Alpha 15 days, at once on AML grounds. Time to dispute a payment: Bank of Cyprus 2 months; Eurobank 60 days, 7 via online banking, or 2 weeks (ex-Eurobank Cyprus terms); Alpha 2 months. All three disclaim the burden of proving authentication. Courts: Cyprus, exclusive only under the ex-Hellenic terms.

Cyprus's capital controls (first decree K.D.P. 98/2013, Gazette of 27 March 2013) ended by expiry, not by a repealing act: the last two Minister of Finance decrees - the 35th decree on transactions (K.D.P. 85/2015) and the 28th decree on foreign banks (K.D.P. 86/2015), both in Gazette No. 4857 of 13 March 2015 - were in force for 21 days from 16 March 2015, i.e. through Sunday 5 April 2015, and were not renewed; Monday 6 April 2015 was the first day without restrictions. By then the 35th decree limited only cashless transfers out of Cyprus (free up to €1,000,000 a month per person per institution) and cash carried abroad above €10,000 per trip, not domestic transfers.

Ending the relationship at Bank of Cyprus (Supplementary Agreement, September 2025, para 19): the customer may terminate in writing at any time; a business that is not a micro-enterprise may be charged even after six months. The bank may close accounts without reason on two months' notice (19.3), at once on listed grounds (19.4), and, 'subject to the provisions of any applicable law', at once where the customer is neither a consumer nor a micro-enterprise (19.7). Grounds include money laundering through an account or the bank's reasonable belief of it (c), 'compliance reasons in accordance with the regulatory framework' (i), and refusal or failure to meet KYC and due-diligence requests (j).

  62. In Central Bank of Cyprus monetary statistics a company is a 'resident of Cyprus' by registration, not by presence. The Bank's statistics chronology (September 2026 edition) records that under the 'Definition of the Term "resident of Cyprus" for Statistical Purposes Directive of 2008', in force from 1 July 2008, enterprises incorporated or registered in Cyprus are residents 'irrespective of whether or not they maintain a physical presence in Cyprus', and that companies with none, 'known as "brass plates"', moved from non-resident to resident. By inference, deposits of a foreign-owned Cyprus-registered company count as domestic, so the non-resident share understates foreign-owned money.

AML, dormancy and set-off in the ex-Hellenic Basic Terms of Eurobank Limited (OP(CD)123 - 5/2025, read 4 Oct 2026): a customer who fails or refuses to supply data requested to update identification or about transactions has the relationship terminated and accounts closed (para 1.3.4(b)).   83. How Bank of Cyprus's termination-for-cause clause acquired its compliance grounds, in three dated editions of its account agreement. The 01/2011 edition (para 22.4; Internet Archive, 1 June 2011) listed death, bankruptcy, dissolution, repeated breach, suspicion or risk of fraud, suspicious transactions and inability to settle - nothing on compliance or due diligence. The April 2018 edition (para 19.4) added 'for compliance reasons', refusal 'to provide important information requested by the Bank in the process of updating his file' and failure to meet its 'Customer Acceptance Policy' criteria. The April 2023 edition recast these as grounds (c), (i), (j): money laundering, compliance, KYC.

How Bank of Cyprus may change terms and fees (Supplementary Agreement, September 2025, para 3): it posts changes on its website or in the press (3.2); a consumer or micro-enterprise is also informed on a durable medium two months before an amendment takes effect, may close the affected accounts in that period without charge, and is deemed to accept if silent; 'where the Customer is neither a Consumer nor a Micro-enterprise, the amendment shall enter into force without prior notice' (3.3) - including fee increases and new fees (3.4). Changes in the customer's favour need no notice (3.5). A micro-enterprise: fewer than ten employees and turnover or balance sheet total not above EUR 2 million.

  1. Cyprus firms read on 6 October 2026 disagree on whether a founder can make the HE1 declaration himself. Harris Koufettas & Associates LLC (FAQ of 20 August 2026) says it 'may be sworn either by that advocate or by a person named in the articles as a director or secretary', and calls the cheapest lawful route paying an advocate for the memorandum and articles and filing HE1-HE3 oneself for €165. EasyCorporate (guide of 13 March 2026) says 'Only licensed lawyers in Cyprus are allowed to sign' HE1; Savva Cyprus that a direct filing by an individual 'will result in the paperwork being rejected'; George K. Konstantinou LLC that the online filing is handled by the lawyer.

Cyprus law has provided since Law 151(I)/2023 (Gazette 19 December 2023) for forming a company 'entirely by electronic means': s. 366E of the Companies Law has the Registrar issue binding directives on online formation that must cover, among other things, 'the role of the practising advocate ... subject to the Advocates Law', and s. 366ΣΤ has him post template memoranda and articles. As read on 6 October 2026, the Registrar's page on incorporation still asks, 'regardless of the type of company', for form HE1 'signed and sworn before the court by the entrusted lawyer' on the e-filing route, and cylaw's indexes of regulatory acts for 2023-2026 list no directive on online formation.

Form HE1 (served 6 October 2026) asks for the 'number of the application for name approval', and his review criteria (page published 28 February 2019, served 6 October 2026) require HE1 and the memorandum to show the company name 'as approved', so both follow the name approval. The memorandum's date must be the date HE1 is submitted to the Department or earlier, and the articles must bear the same date and the name and signature of the lawyer who drew them up, so the signed documents exist by the filing. No text read orders the swearing of HE1 against the signing of the memorandum and articles.

  6. A founder may be his own Cyprus company's secretary without a licence only within two limits. Cap. 113 s. 171(1) requires a secretary and bars a sole director from being also secretary, except in a private company with a single member. Law 196(I)/2012 s. 4(3)(β) (cylaw text amended to Law 69(I)/2025, read 6 October 2026) frees a natural person resident in Cyprus from the administrative-services licence to act as secretary where the company is at least 50% owned by him, his spouse or relatives to the fourth degree - 25% where the shareholders are Cyprus-resident individuals - or is his sole employer, if the service is not advertised or offered to others.

A company struck off the Cyprus register under s. 327 of the Companies Law, Cap. 113 - as in the unpaid-levy round starting in December 2026 - is dissolved on publication of the strike-off notice, but any liability of its directors, officers and members continues (s. 327(5) proviso). The company, a member, a creditor or a person harmed by its acts before the strike-off may apply to the court to restore it within twenty years of publication of the strike-off; the court may restore it if it was carrying on business or if restoration is just, and may order payment of the fees owed to the Registrar and of his costs (s. 327(7)). Cylaw consolidated text read 6 October 2026.

Reading the Cyprus texts together for a founder paid a salary by his own private company (inference, 5 October 2026): the Social Insurance Law counts a shareholder's work in his private company as employment, so the company applies to the Social Insurance Services at least one day before he starts, gets an employer number, opens an Ergani account and notifies his hiring a day ahead; it files employer returns with the Tax Department through Tax For All (subject to that page's carve-out); he gives it form T.D.59 each year.   40. A legal person may be director or secretary of a Cyprus company. The Companies Law (Cap. 113) assumes it: s. 192(2)(β) and (3)(β) prescribe what the register of directors and secretaries records for a director or secretary that is a legal person (corporate name and registered office; for a director, registered or principal office), and s. 172 only forbids two combinations - a corporate secretary whose sole director is the company's sole director, and a corporate sole director whose sole director is the company's secretary - neither applying to a single-member private company. No provision of the Cyprus Companies Law (Cap. 113) obliges a company to engage a licensed accountant for bookkeeping: s. 141(1) puts the duty to keep accounting books on the directors, and s. 141(4) accepts as a defence that a competent and reliable person was charged with it (cylaw consolidated text, read 4 Oct 2026). Licensed professionals enter elsewhere: the yearly audit or review needs a statutory auditor (s. 152A), and under s. 29 of Law 4/1978, as replaced by Law 243(I)/2025 from 1 January 2026, the tax authority may disregard accounts not prepared and certified by a statutory auditor and tax computations not prepared and certified by a holder of an ICPAC practising certificate.

Before its repeal on 1 January 2026 the Cyprus Stamp Duty Law (19/1963) charged nothing specific on forming a company: its First Schedule, as last consolidated on cylaw (35 items, amendments to Law 221(I)/2025), names no memorandum, articles, share capital or incorporation; only partnership deeds are named (item 20). Generic items remained: a written affidavit or formal declaration €4 (item 2), an agreement without a stated sum €35 (item 3B), an attested document not otherwise covered €2 (item 32). The memorandum had to be stamped 'as an agreement' until Law 149(I)/2018 deleted that from s. 5 of the Companies Law. What the Registrar actually collected in 2019-2025 was not established.

Who may not be a director of a Cyprus company (Companies Law, Cap. 113, read 4 Oct 2026): an undischarged bankrupt, without leave of the bankruptcy court (s. 179, an offence); a person whom a court - after conviction for an offence tied to promoting, forming or managing a company, or a finding in a winding-up of fraud or breach of duty as an officer - has barred, save with its leave, from being a director or taking part in management for up to five years (s. 180). Since Law 151(I)/2023 (19.12.2023) the Registrar may also reject the appointment of a person disqualified in another EU Member State, and the Registrar or anyone with a legitimate interest may ask the court to end it (s. 180Α).

  75. The Cyprus Registrar's €165 total for registering a company exceeds the €105 registration item of its fee schedule by €60, and as of 4 Oct 2026 the Registrar publishes only the total. The schedule (K.D.P. 31/2013, Part I, item 3 after the renumbering by K.D.P. 364/2018) has two filing items that can build it: 3(θ) 'statutory declaration' €40 and 3(ι) 'any document required by the Law ... for which no other provision is made' €20. Two splits give €165: 105 + 40 (HE1 as statutory declaration) + 20, or 105 + 3 x 20 (HE1, HE2, HE3). The Registrar charges €20 more for form HE5 of a public company and €20 for HE2 or HE4 filed alone, which fits the per-form reading without proving it.

  1. Cyprus VAT attaches to the person, whatever the rung. Under VAT Law 95(I)/2000 a taxable person is 'every person who is registered or required to be registered' (s. 6(1)); 'legal person' includes a partnership, whether or not constituted under any law (s. 2). Persons carrying on business in partnership may be registered in the firm's name, and until the Commissioner is told of a change, a partner who has left is treated as still a partner, in particular for liability for VAT on the firm's supplies (s. 34(1)-(2)). Read in the consolidated text on 6 October 2026.

  6. A seller established in Cyprus that uses the EU One Stop Shop (Union scheme) is identified there by the VAT number Cyprus has already given it. Article 369d of VAT Directive 2006/112/EC (consolidated version of 14 April 2025, read 6 October 2026) says the Member State of identification 'shall use the individual VAT identification number already allocated to the taxable person in respect of his obligations under the internal system'. On that wording, Cyprus VAT registration comes before OSS use; the Commission's Cyprus OSS page does not say so itself.

An online shop's registration in the EU One Stop Shop (union scheme) comes after its Cyprus VAT registration: under art. 369d of VAT Directive 2006/112/EC (in force; consolidated text of 14 April 2025 read 6 October 2026) the Member State of identification uses 'the individual VAT identification number already allocated' to the trader under the domestic system. The scheme is one Member States 'shall permit' traders to use (art. 369b), not a duty; it becomes relevant once intra-EU distance sales to consumers exceed €10,000 in a calendar year, or the seller opts to tax them at destination, when they are taxed in the customer's Member State (art. 59c).

  9. Splitting one business among two or more persons to stay under the Cyprus VAT threshold can be overridden. Under para. 2 of Part I of the First Schedule to VAT Law 95(I)/2000 (consolidated text read 6 October 2026) the Commissioner may direct that the persons named be treated as a single taxable person liable to register, from the date of the direction or a later date it sets. He may name a person only if satisfied that the person makes taxable supplies in activities that properly belong to one business carried on with others, that the whole would be liable to register, and that avoiding registration is the main reason or one of the main reasons for the arrangement.

  11. Cyprus law times compulsory VAT registration from the trigger, not from incorporation. Under the First Schedule, Part I, of VAT Law 95(I)/2000 (cylaw text read 6 October 2026) a person established in Cyprus whose taxable supplies in the year to a month's end exceeded the threshold must notify the Commissioner within thirty days from the end of that month and is registered from the end of the next month or an agreed earlier date (paras 1(1)(α), 5), unless the Commissioner accepts that the coming year will stay below the lower limit (para 1(3)); one expecting to exceed it in the next thirty days notifies before they end and is registered from their start (paras 1(1)(β), 6).

The Cyprus Tax Department's VAT Leaflet 3 'Registration in the VAT Register' (November 2001, still linked from its VAT registration page on 5 Oct 2026) says what an intending trader must show: a business that has started but makes no taxable supplies yet may register if it intends to make them, and must send written evidence, which 'may include' details of arrangements made, copies of proposed contracts, building permits, details of purchases made for the business, or patent applications; without it the examination 'may be delayed'. On timing it says only that the registration number and certificate come once the examination is completed. It is guidance of 2001, naming the old form VAT 101.

  15. The first VAT return of a Cyprus company registered in late 2026 falls due by the quarter given at registration, normally by NACE activity code. Reg. 17(1) of the VAT Regulations K.D.P. 314/2001 requires each return by the tenth day after the end of the month following the period; proviso (β): the first return covers the scheduled period in which the person was registered, starting that day. The Tax Department's 2026 calendar shows three staggered sets of quarters and moves a weekend or holiday due date to the next working day. A period ending 30 November 2026 falls due on 11 January 2027 (the 10th is a Sunday), one ending 31 December on 10 February, one ending 31 January on 10 March.

Interpretative Circular 161 of 13 January 2012 (VAT Service, then part of the Customs Department) announced that, under para 1A of the Tenth Schedule to the VAT Law and reg. 13A of K.D.P. 314/2001 (inserted by K.D.P. 536/2011, Gazette No. 4539 of 30 December 2011), from that date every taxable person making a taxable supply to a non-taxable person in Cyprus issues and delivers a VAT receipt at the time of supply.   23. The VAT exemption for payments and transfers (art. 135(1)(d) of Directive 2006/112/EC, ex art. 13B(d)(3) of the Sixth Directive) is read narrowly by the Court of Justice. Under the Sixth Directive, SDC (C-2/95, 5 June 1997) - an outsourced service is exempt only if, viewed broadly, it forms a distinct whole fulfilling the specific, essential functions of a transfer, not a mere physical or technical supply; Nordea (C-350/10, 28 July 2011) - SWIFT messaging not exempt. Under art. 135(1)(d): Bookit (C-607/14, 26 May 2016) - a 'card handling' fee on a cinema ticket paid by card is not exempt; DPAS (C-5/17, 25 July 2018) - asking banks to run direct debits and onward transfers is not exempt.

  24. Two Court of Justice judgments of 2010 on payment handling. AXA UK (C-175/09, 28 October 2010): a service that consists, in essence, in asking a third party's bank to transfer by direct debit a sum due to the supplier's client, reporting receipts, chasing non-payers and passing on the money less a fee is not covered by the exemption of art. 13B(d)(3) of the Sixth Directive (it is debt collection). Everything Everywhere (C-276/09, 2 December 2010): extra charges a telecoms provider invoices to customers who pay by credit card, debit card, cheque or cash rather than direct debit are not consideration for a separate supply; they share the VAT treatment of the principal supply.

  25. For a shop, the commission kept by the card company does not reduce the VAT base. In Chaussures Bally (C-18/92, judgment of 25 May 1993) the Court of Justice held, on art. 11A(1)(a) of the Sixth VAT Directive (now art. 73 of Directive 2006/112/EC), that where the purchaser pays by credit card and the card-issuing organisation pays the supplier the price after deducting a percentage as commission for the service it renders to the supplier, the sum so deducted must be included in the taxable amount on which the supplier pays VAT. A merchant therefore accounts for output VAT on the full price charged to the customer, not on the amount settled after the merchant service charge.

Cyprus VAT Circular 156 of 11 October 2011 follows the Court of Justice in Nordea (C-350/10): SWIFT services are electronic messaging, cause no legal or financial change between the parties, and are not exempt. A person established in Cyprus that receives them accounts for output VAT at the standard rate (then 15%) by reverse charge. Where a financial institution uses them for a money-movement service exempt under para 3(γ) of Table B of the Seventh Schedule, they are an inseparable part of that single supply and cannot be invoiced separately. It adds that Member States are in principle bound to apply the reading retroactively; in Cyprus the provision dates from 1 February 2002.

  61. VAT registration in Cyprus (Tax Department page read on 4 October 2026): a person established in Cyprus must register when taxable supplies in the 12 months ending at any month-end exceeded €15,600, or when there are reasonable grounds to believe they will exceed €15,600 in the next 30 days; capital assets are not counted. Separate triggers: intra-EU acquisitions above €10,251.61 in a calendar year; supplying services to taxable persons in another Member State where the recipient accounts for the VAT there — no threshold, registration from the first transaction plus VIES recapitulative statements; persons not established in Cyprus — no threshold. Late notification costs €85 per month. Voluntary registration is allowed below the threshold.

CESOP: Directive (EU) 2020/284 (applied by Member States from 1 January 2024) obliges payment service providers to keep quarterly records of payees and cross-border payments once they provide more than 25 cross-border payments to the same payee in a calendar quarter. Cyprus transposed it by VAT (Amendment) Law 10(I)/2024 and Regulations K.D.P. 52/2024, both published 23 February 2024; the Regulations are deemed in force from 1 January 2024 (reg. 7) and require the records to be submitted to the Tax Commissioner by the end of the month after each quarter. Failure to submit carries a €15,000 charge (VAT Law art. 45(7Γ)). Filing is through the Tax Department's CESOP portal.

  2. Cyprus social insurance bases differ by rung. Under s. 2 of the Social Insurance Law 59(I)/2010 (consolidated text, 6 October 2026) an employed person's 'earnings' are his money pay and money-valued gains from it (less extraordinary commissions and ex-gratia payments); a self-employed person's are 'every profit and gain' from his work, computed as Regulations set (s. 78) - from a category minimum unless lower income is proved. Both count only up to the insurable-earnings ceiling; neither names dividends. A pension-reform draft bill (consulted 2-16 September 2026; not tabled by 6 October 2026) would add 'every dividend' a shareholder employed by his own private company receives from it.

  12. Self-employed insurance in Cyprus does not count towards unemployment benefit: under s. 24(2)(α) of the Social Insurance Law 59(I)/2010 (consolidated text read 6 October 2026) self-employed periods 'are not taken into account for the purposes of unemployment benefit'. A founder working for his own private company is insured as employed (First Schedule, Part I, para. 5). A day counts as unemployment only if the claimant proves he is unemployed, capable of and available for work (or in approved training); a day of gainful occupation does not count unless he could normally do it besides his usual work, outside its hours, and earns no more than a prescribed amount that day (s. 31(4)(β), (ε)).

  13. Two rules of Cyprus's Social Insurance Law 59(I)/2010 (First Schedule, consolidated text read 6 October 2026) separate the rungs. Employment 'in the service of the spouse' of the person employed is an excepted, non-insurable employment (Part II, para. 3), so a sole trader's husband or wife working for him or her is not insured as an employee. Employment of a person 'under any circumstances' in a private company in which he is a shareholder is insurable employment as an employed person (Part I, para. 5); the paragraph names private companies within the Companies Law only, not partnerships.

  18. Officers of a Cyprus company can answer personally for its social insurance offences. Under s. 85(9) of the Social Insurance Law 59(I)/2010 (consolidated text read 6 October 2026), where an offence under the Law or its Regulations is committed by a legal person and is shown to have been committed with the consent, connivance or negligence of a director, manager, secretary or similar officer, both that person and the legal person are guilty of it. Failing or neglecting to pay any contribution is itself an offence (up to one year's imprisonment, a €3,400 fine or both, s. 85(1)); on conviction the employer must also pay the unpaid contributions plus up to 25% as the Court orders (s. 85(2)).

How a fine for undeclared work runs in Cyprus (Social Insurance Law 59(I)/2010, read 5 Oct 2026): the inspector serves a notice of the finding on the spot and the employer has five days for representations (s. 85Α(4)); the fine is payable within 30 days of service of the fining act (s. 85Ζ), is cut by 30% if paid in time and grows by €50 per day of delay (s. 85Α(6)). An objection goes to an Objections Committee within 15 days and does not suspend the decision (s. 85Θ). After a second fine within two years a committee may, with the Minister's consent, suspend all or part of the business for up to 48 hours (s. 85Γ(1)). Households employing domestic workers or carers are exempt (s. 85Α(7)).

An employer in Cyprus pays social insurance and the other payroll-fund contributions by the end of the calendar month after the month for which they are due - on the next working day if that day is a Saturday, Sunday or holiday (Social Insurance Services' Employer Guide, PDF of 2 June 2025; their web page of 23 March 2021 has the month-end rule). Late payment bears an additional charge on social insurance, social cohesion and health-system contributions: 3% for up to a month, 3 points more per further month or part of one, at most 27%. A first payroll for November 2026 is thus payable by 31 December 2026; the Tax Department's calendar puts the GeSY contribution for November on the same day.

Cyprus's Social Insurance Law 59(I)/2010 has no rule for third-country nationals as such (text read 5 October 2026): insurable employment turns on work in Cyprus (First Schedule, Part I, para 1). Part II, para 4 excludes by residence, not nationality: a person not ordinarily resident in Cyprus or another Member State employed by an employer with no residence, seat or place of business in Cyprus. Only the Services' Employer Guide (PDF of 2 June 2025) names them: 'international activities companies' owe contributions for all employees, but third-country employees who prove to the Director, on application, that they are not ordinarily resident in Cyprus are exempted. It cites no legal basis.

  29. Cyprus law fixes no minimum insurable earnings for a shareholder employed by his own company. Section 4 of Law 59(I)/2010 makes contributions due for each period in which a person was employed as an employed person 'except where the earnings of the employed person are negligible'; reg. 7 of the Contributions Regulations (K.D.P. 289/2010) puts negligible below €2 a week or €7 a month. Deemed earnings exist only for apprentices and prisoners (s. 5(3)-(4)). Notional minimums by occupational category apply to the self-employed alone (reg. 16). Read on 5 October 2026 in the Law, K.D.P. 289/2010 and its amendments K.D.P. 398/2013 and 167/2017; the Services' June 2025 guides add nothing.

Under Cyprus's Social Insurance Law 59(I)/2010 a person who works for a private company in which he holds shares is an employed person, not a self-employed one: paragraph 5 of Part I of the First Schedule lists as insurable employment of an employed person the 'employment of a person under any circumstances in a private company in which he is a shareholder', 'private company' having the Companies Law meaning. The self-employed are defined by exclusion (Second Schedule, Part I): work for gain in Cyprus that is not insurable under Part I of the First Schedule. The rule does not depend on nationality or on the size of the shareholding. Read in the consolidated text on 5 October 2026.

Actuarial valuation of Cyprus's General Social Insurance Scheme as of 31 December 2020 (ILO report ILO/TF/Cyprus/R.27, copyright 2024, on the Social Insurance Services' site): Table A1.2 gives the legislated contribution rates for employed persons as 8.8% employee + 8.8% employer + 5.2% State = 22.8% for 2024–2028; 9.3% + 9.3% + 5.5% = 24.1% for 2029–2033; 9.8% + 9.8% + 5.8% = 25.4% for 2034–2038; 10.3% + 10.3% + 6.1% = 26.7% from 2039. The report concludes that this schedule, following the 2009 and 2012 reforms, is sufficient for the long-term benefits branch over 2021–2080. These are the future steps quoted in the Services' Employer Guide, not the higher ones printed in Law 59(I)/2010.

Art. 5(1)(ζ) and art. 12(η) of Law 59(I)/2010, as replaced by Law 126(I)/2019 (Gazette No. 4725, 5 August 2019), print 9.5% each for employee and employer and 18% for the self-employed, but two provisos say (1) if an actuarial study before a step shows that no increase, or a smaller one, is needed, the rates it indicates apply, and (2) the increases may not be lower than the rates in force just before the 2019 Law. Failure to notify a hire in Cyprus is 'undeclared work': s. 2 of the Social Insurance Law 59(I)/2010 defines it as insurable employment not declared to the Director under reg. 5(1) (employees) or reg. 4(3) (self-employed) of the Contributions Regulations. Under s. 85Α(1) an inspector fines the employer €1,000 per undeclared employee for the month of detection (€500 until Law 127(I)/2024, 15 November 2024) plus €500 per earlier calendar month or part of it; s. 85Β presumes six earlier months unless the employer proves less. Repeats within two years: €2,000, then €3,000 (s. 85Α(1Α)). Up to ten insured persons: cap €10,000 per finding (s. 85Α(3)). Introduced by Law 52(I)/2017. Read 4 Oct 2026.

  2. Adyen's documentation ('Deposit', docs.adyen.com, read 5 October 2026) gives mechanics its terms leave out. The deposit requirement is recalculated daily before payout as estimated exposure - orders paid but unfulfilled plus chargebacks and refunds predicted from the past 180 days - against coverage: pending and payable balances, any bank guarantee, the existing deposit and an 'accepted risk' set case by case. Funds are withheld from the next payout only when exposure exceeds coverage by more than EUR 10,000. A bank guarantee or standby letter of credit may replace the deposit in part or in full. The deposit is 'exclusively owned by you' and returned about six months after processing stops.
