SumUp's Cyprus help article on chargebacks - the page its Payment Terms (section 16) point to for chargeback charges - says 'payment providers charge a non-refundable fee of €10 for chargebacks' (undated, read 5 October 2026). SumUp first covers the chargeback and takes the amount out of the merchant's next scheduled payout; the merchant must send evidence within the deadline set by the acquiring bank; if the issuing bank decides for the merchant, SumUp keeps the money for 60 days, until the cardholder's objection period ends, and then returns it.

  6. Four of the changes between JCC's Terms Version 1.3 (January 2015) and 2.8 (2023).   8. For a Cyprus user the Stripe Services Agreement (General Terms last modified 28 September 2026) is governed by the laws of Ireland. Disputes go to binding arbitration by a single arbitrator in Dublin, administered by the ICC International Court of Arbitration; the arbitrator must be a member of the Law Society of Ireland or the Bar of Ireland unless the parties agree otherwise. Claims that may not be arbitrated, including intellectual-property claims, go to the courts of Ireland, and Stripe may still bring insolvency proceedings 'in an appropriate court under insolvency laws in the User's jurisdiction'. PayPal's user agreement for Cyprus (last updated 7 September 2026) makes the seller liable for a reversed payment by default: 'If you receive a payment in your account, you owe us the full amount of the payment and our losses arising from processing the payment (including any Chargeback fee or Dispute fee)'. PayPal sets these amounts off against the balance, converting other balances if needed. The stated exception is PayPal's Seller Protection programme, under which an eligible seller may keep the full purchase amount. For a card-funded payment the card issuer, not PayPal, decides the chargeback, and PayPal may hold money until the chargeback risk under card-scheme rules has passed.

The European Commission opened an infringement against Cyprus over investor citizenship on 20 October 2020, holding that granting nationality, and so EU citizenship, for a pre-determined payment without a 'genuine link' breaches sincere cooperation (Art. 4(3) TEU) and undermines EU citizenship. Cyprus's legal basis for forming a company online, Law 151(I)/2023 (Gazette 19 December 2023), was adopted to transpose Directive (EU) 2019/1151 on digital tools in company law, per the House Commerce Committee's report of 6 December 2023. It provides online formation and online registration of a foreign company's branch, free model documents, the Registrar's power to refuse a director disqualified in another member state, and electronic identification of EU citizens using the Registrar's online services. Why Cyprus closed its beneficial-owner register to the general public (Law 25(I)/2026, Gazette 20 March 2026): the Finance Minister's letter tabling the bill (19 December 2025) says it transposes Article 74 of Directive (EU) 2024/1640, which aims at compliance with the CJEU's WM and Sovim judgment that unrestricted public access breaches the rights to private life and data protection. The Ministry of Finance's reasons for Cyprus's 2026 tax reform, in its introductory report (30 October 2025) and impact questionnaire on the income tax bill: the aim is 'a fairer tax system' that burdens economic strata proportionally and reduces inequalities; the last broad reform was in 2002, for EU harmonisation, and since then the environment 'has changed radically', so 'an integrated tax transformation' is required; economic and social bodies had called for reform as more than 23 years had passed; it was in the President's election programme.   1. Amendment No. 1 to the Fourth Issue of the Central Bank of Cyprus AML directive (circular letter SD 6020) took effect on 7 April 2016, on publication on the Bank's website. It added para 76A (audited accounts, or management accounts, from customers); paras 85A-86E on customers introduced by third parties (reliance only at the outset; a meeting with the beneficial owners within three months, in person or online with recording; termination if it cannot be held; a scorecard and register of introducers); and paras 128A-128B (a face-to-face meeting within three months for non-face-to-face customers with account debits or credits above EUR 100,000 a year).   6. Shell companies: on 2 November 2018 the Central Bank of Cyprus sent a circular (ref. BS 6020), effective at once, to all credit, payment and e-money institutions, after a first one of 14 June 2018. A shell company has no physical presence and no established economic activity in its country of incorporation (holding shares or assets may count as activity). Relationships 'shall be avoided' if it also is registered where audited accounts are not required and prepares none voluntarily, and/or is tax resident in an EU- or OECD-blacklisted jurisdiction or nowhere; otherwise the institution decides on a documented risk basis. The CBC's February 2019 AML directive revoked it and absorbed its rules.

  7. Cyprus Law 188(I)/2007 art. 64 requires enhanced due diligence for business with high-risk third countries, for cross-border correspondent relationships and for politically exposed persons. For a PEP - and for close relatives and known close associates - the obliged entity must obtain senior-management approval to establish or continue the relationship, take adequate measures to establish the source of wealth and source of funds, and conduct enhanced ongoing monitoring (art. 64(1)(c)). Art. 63 allows simplified measures only after the entity has satisfied itself that the relationship is lower-risk and there is no suspicion. In force on 4 October 2026.

Law 13(I)/2021 (5AMLD transposition, 23 February 2021) inserted art. 61Δ into Cyprus Law 188(I)/2007, creating a Central Register of Bank Accounts, Payment Accounts and Safe Deposit Boxes kept electronically by the Central Bank of Cyprus. Institutions supervised by the CBC supply, for every IBAN-identified bank or payment account and every safe-deposit box, the identification data of the holder, of any person acting for the holder and of the beneficial owner, the IBAN and the dates of opening and closing. MOKAS, the Police, the Tax Department and the Customs Department may search it directly. In force on 4 October 2026; the date the register became operational was not established.

  19. Cyprus Law 188(I)/2007 art. 62(1) requires the identity of the customer and the beneficial owner to be verified before a business relationship is established or a transaction is carried out. Derogations: verification may be completed during the establishment of the relationship if needed not to interrupt normal business and the risk is low (art. 62(2)); an account may be opened provided no transactions take place until due diligence is complete (art. 62(3)). If due diligence cannot be completed the entity must not transact or open, must terminate, and considers a report to MOKAS (art. 62(4)). Records are kept five years after the relationship ends (art. 68(1)). In force on 4 October 2026.

Law 172(I)/2024 (published 31 December 2024; in force on publication) inserted Article 2B into the Cyprus AML Law 188(I)/2007: persons trading in goods or providing services, including the purchase and sale of real estate, may receive or pay cash only up to EUR 10,000, in one or more linked operations; 'cash' includes bearer negotiable instruments, highly liquid commodities and prepaid cards. Cyprus Law 188(I)/2007 art. 2(1) defines 'politically exposed persons' as a natural person who is or has been entrusted with a prominent public function 'in the Republic or in another country', an immediate close relative, and a person known as a close associate - so domestic office-holders are covered. The listed functions include heads of state and government, ministers, members of parliament, governing bodies of political parties, senior judges, central-bank boards, boards of state enterprises and mayors; middle and junior officials are excluded. After the person leaves office the risk is considered for at least 12 months (art. 64(1)(c) proviso). In force on 4 October 2026.

Art. 2(1) of Cyprus Law 188(I)/2007 defines the beneficial owner of a legal person as the natural person who ultimately owns or controls it through a sufficient percentage of shares, voting rights or ownership interest, or by other means; companies listed on a regulated market are excepted. A holding of 25% plus one share, or an ownership interest above 25%, held directly or indirectly, is an 'indication' of ownership. Only if all possible means are exhausted, there are no grounds for suspicion and nobody is identified - or the person identified is in doubt - is the senior managing official treated as beneficial owner. In force on 4 October 2026; the 2024-2026 amendments did not touch it.

  35. MOKAS, the Cyprus financial intelligence unit, is the 'Unit for Combating Money Laundering and Financial Intelligence Unit' established by art. 54 of the AML Law 188(I)/2007. It is composed of representatives of the Attorney General, the Chief of Police and the Director of Customs, is headed by the Attorney General's representative, and under art. 55 is operationally independent. It receives suspicious transaction reports from obliged entities; it does not license or supervise firms — supervision belongs to the authorities listed in art. 59. Consolidated text read on 4 October 2026 (amended up to Law 25(I)/2026).

  36. Art. 61Δ of Cyprus Law 188(I)/2007 (in force 4 October 2026) is silent on telling an account holder that the Central Register of Bank Accounts was searched: no duty to notify and, unlike arts. 61A(7) and 61B(7) on the beneficial-owner registers, no 'without notification' clause. Its safeguard is a log: the Central Bank records every access (date and time, data used, authority, user), has it checked by its data protection officer, gives it to the data protection Commissioner on request and deletes entries after five years unless an audit is under way (61Δ(5), added by Law 40(I)/2022). For the National Sanctions Implementation Unit, Law 150(I)/2025 s. 18(d) rules out notifying the holder.

Having no commencement clause, it took effect on publication (Constitution, Art. 82). Law 98(I)/2023 (Official Gazette no. 4960, 20 October 2023) amended Cyprus Law 188(I)/2007 with one stated purpose: compliance with the FATF standards referred to in MONEYVAL's second follow-up technical-compliance report on Cyprus, 'published in November 2022' (preamble). It redefined which crypto-asset service providers are obliged entities and must register (arts. 2A, 61E), extended enhanced due diligence to all cross-border correspondent relationships, not only third-country ones (art. 64(1)(b)), and rewrote the new-technologies risk duty (art. 66(2A)). It is not the only amendment citing MONEYVAL: Law 96(I)/2025 (18 June 2025) names the third report (December 2023) among five purposes.

  3. Remote account opening in Cyprus predates the 2025 directive and eIDAS. The Central Bank of Cyprus Guidance Note of November 1999 had non-residents 'who wish to open bank accounts by post' verified through a credit or financial institution in their country. Its directives of April 2008 and December 2013 let a customer 'request the opening of an account through mail, telephone, or the internet without presenting himself for a personal interview', with enhanced checks (2013: bank confirmation, or a verified phone call plus a registered letter). From 7 April 2016 (Amendment No. 1) such customers with account debits or credits over EUR 100,000 a year had to be met in person within three months.

  6. Video entered the Central Bank of Cyprus AML directive on 7 April 2016. Amendment No. 1 to the Fourth Issue (new para 86A) obliged a bank to meet face to face a customer introduced by a third party - for a legal person, its beneficial owners or controllers - within three months of account opening, adding: 'The meeting may be held over the internet on condition that adequate safeguards are in place such as sound / video recording of the meeting.' The Fifth Edition of February 2019 (para 119) kept the sentence and moved the meeting to 'before executing any transaction'; it has no section on non-face-to-face customers. MONEYVAL's 2019 report dates the two requirements to 2016 and 2019.

Central Bank of Cyprus AML Directive of 2025 (in force since 2 June 2025), para 50(3): a relationship or transaction 'relates to' a high-risk third country if the funds were generated in, are received from or are destined for one, if the customer is a natural person or legal entity resident or established there, or if a trustee is established there or the trust is governed by its law. The 2019 text (paras 254-255) accepted copies certified by the bank's employee or by a third party the bank relied on and, for non-Cypriot persons and foreign entities, apostilled originals.   32. Remote onboarding in Cyprus rests on two layers. Law 188(I)/2007 art. 61(1)(a) accepts identification by electronic identification means and trust services under Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 or by any other secure remote or electronic identification process regulated, recognised, approved or accepted by a competent authority of the Republic. The CBC Directive of 2025 (paras 27-28 and 59(1)(g), in force since 2 June 2025) obliges institutions to comply with EBA Guidelines EBA/GL/2022/15 on remote customer onboarding and defines 'non-face to face customers' as including those whose identity is verified 'via a video link or similar technological means'.

Under para 27 of the Central Bank of Cyprus AML Directive of 2025 (K.D.P. 120/2025, in force since 2 June 2025) a relationship started 'remotely (without the physical presence of the parties)' is not high-risk by default: the institution must assess whether it creates an increased risk and adapt its measures if so (27(1)(b)); enhanced due diligence under para 42 applies only where that risk is high (27(2)); and electronic identification means do not create an increased risk, in particular where they give a high level of assurance under Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 (27(4)). Remote customers are not among the four categories for which para 42(2) makes enhanced due diligence mandatory.

Cyprus restricts land acquisition by 'aliens' under the Immovable Property Acquisition (Aliens) Law, Cap. 109: an alien may not acquire immovable property, otherwise than on death, without the Council of Ministers' prior permission (s. 3(1)); a registration in breach is void (s. 3(5)). 'Alien' means a non-citizen and includes an alien-controlled company, a foreign company and a trust for an alien; it excludes an 'alien Cypriot' (non-citizen of Cypriot birth or descent as defined), a non-citizen wife of a citizen not separated by court decision, EU and EEA citizens, and legal persons formed under another EU state's law and seated in the EEA (s. 2). Under Law 45(I)/2019 on sworn translators (unamended on CyLaw, 6 October 2026), a 'certified translation' is a valid and accurate translation between a foreign language and Greek or Turkish, bearing the Republic's official seal and duly stamped, made by a sworn translator on the Council's Register (s. 2). Foreign-language official documents are entered in public registers after translation by a sworn translator into an official language (s. 18). An advocate not on the Register may translate only for his own cases, accepted exceptionally with a sworn statement of the reason (s. 14(2)); the Registrar's pages accept a Greek translation 'by an affidavit in court' or by a sworn translator.

Time limits in Cyprus's foreign-investment screening Law 194(I)/2025 (s. 5): within 20 working days of a complete application the Ministry of Finance decides whether the investment will be screened and tells the investor within 5 working days; if it screens, it decides within 65 working days whether the investment may harm security or public order. The duty also reaches an entity at least 25%-owned, beneficially owned or controlled by a foreign investor that invests in an undertaking of strategic importance (s. 3(6)); the Ministry's guidance of 28 July 2026 (Q3.6) applies this to entities incorporated in Cyprus, the EU, the EEA or Switzerland. Neither text mentions residence: on their wording a third-country national living in Cyprus is a foreign investor.

Signatures and seals on documents in Cyprus are certified by certifying officers appointed by the Interior Minister under Law 165(I)/2012, at least one per municipal parish; a practising lawyer, estate agent or banker may not be one (s. 3(4)). The Law set €2 per signature or seal (s. 10(1)); the Minister's notice K.D.P. 48/2024 (Gazette No. 5856, 16 February 2024) replaced this with maximum fees per document: €5 for 1-2 pages, €10 for 3-10, €25 for 11-100, €40 above, plus at most €2 per extra signer or seal, and at most €10 for travel. For private documents sent abroad, such as powers of attorney, it sends further certification to the Justice Ministry or citizen service centres.

A Cyprus municipality also charges each legal person trading within its limits an annual fee (Municipalities Law 52(I)/2022, s. 56(6)) up to Sixth Schedule ceilings: a private company with up to 5 employees EUR 1,000, rising to EUR 4,000 over 30; partnerships EUR 1,000-5,000; insurance, shipping, banking and like firms and public companies EUR 10,000; legal persons whose registered office or management is with law, accounting or audit firms or administrative-service providers EUR 4,000; others EUR 1,500. Half if business starts in the second half-year; another municipality may charge only where the company has a permanent place of business there or works there over 60 working days a year.

The new Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853 must be in force in national law by 9 December 2026 and applies to products placed on the market or put into service after 8 December 2026 (a corrigendum of 7 May 2026 replaced 'after 9 December'); the 1985 Directive keeps covering earlier products. For an online shop it widens who answers: where the maker is outside the EU, the importer and the authorised representative or, failing both, the fulfilment service provider (art. 8(1)(c)); where no EU operator can be identified, a distributor that fails within a month of a request to name one or its own supplier is liable (art. 8(3)). Cylaw's 2026 list shows no Cyprus transposing law.

The first ViDA stage relevant to small online sellers is 1 January 2027: Member States must adopt and publish rules transposing Article 2 of Council Directive (EU) 2025/516 by 31 December 2026 and apply them from 1 January 2027. Among other points, Article 2 limits the EUR 10,000 threshold of art. 59c of the VAT Directive to goods dispatched from the seller's own Member State, and deems a seller registered in the union one-stop shop to have opted for taxation in the customer's state. Cylaw's 2025-2026 lists (to 2 October 2026) show no transposing law; the only 2026 VAT amendment, Law 109(I)/2026, lets the Tax Commissioner examine delayed reduced-rate housing applications until end-2026.

The EU Pay Transparency Directive (EU) 2023/970 had to be transposed by 7 June 2026 (art. 34(1)); it gives job applicants a right to information on the initial pay or its range, for example in the vacancy notice or before the interview, and bars employers from asking about pay history (art. 5), with no size threshold. Cyprus has not enacted it as of 6 October 2026: the draft bill was consulted on from 5 November to 4 December 2025 ('completed'; results and a revised draft posted), CyLaw's 2026 laws (to Law 128(I)/2026) have none, and the Gazette search finds '2023/970' only in tender notices. By our reading, art. 5 binds a private employer only once the Cyprus law is in force.

Under eIDAS as amended by Regulation (EU) 2024/1183, each Member State must provide at least one EU Digital Identity Wallet within 24 months of the entry into force of the implementing acts under arts 5a(23) and 5c(6) (Implementing Regulations 2024/2977, 2979, 2980, 2981, 2982; in force 24.12.2024): by our count 24 December 2026. From 10 July 2027 the EU AML Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 binds legal entities created in the Union directly: obtain accurate, up-to-date beneficial-owner information within 28 calendar days of creation, update it within 28 days of a change and yearly (art. 62(2)); report it to the central register 'without undue delay' after creation, and any change within 28 calendar days (art. 63(2)). A Cyprus company now has 90 days from incorporation to file and 45 days for a change (K.D.P. 112/2021 paras 9(1), 10(2), as amended by K.D.P. 34/2024). The change window will shorten; for the first report the Regulation fixes no number of days. No Cyprus act adjusting this was found as of 6 October 2026.

Under rule 84B of the Rules of Procedure of the Cyprus House of Representatives (published in the Gazette on 1 November 2019; parliament.cy unofficial codification of January 2020), members' bills pending before a committee at the end of a parliamentary term whose discussion has not yet begun, and members' bills tabled by MPs who were not re-elected, are deemed withdrawn at the start of the new term and struck off the committee's agenda; reviving one needs a new tabling. The rule names only members' bills, not government bills or regulations. A Nomoplatform 'pending' label on such a bill after the May 2026 elections is therefore not proof that it is live. Cyprus's 2018 rules on lawyers' out-of-court fees (K.D.P. 171/2018, adopted by the Bar's extraordinary general meeting on 19 June 2018) let the client fix the price in writing: an advocate must otherwise claim a fee set by the regulations' criteria for a reasonable fee (regs 4, 10), but is released from that if the client signs an 'Advocate Appointment Form' or agreement containing the provisions of Annex I (reg 5(1)(a)). Annex I names the client and the advocate or law office, describes the matter, states the fee the client agrees to pay and how it will be paid, and is signed by the client. Documents an advocate drafts in such matters carry his name, office, signature and stamp (reg 17).

  4. What a hired lawyer or provider cannot close in Cyprus, read from the sources as of 6 October 2026. The bank decides whether to open an account: the right to a basic payment account covers consumers, not businesses, and provider schedules read sell only an 'application' with no guaranteed success. Beneficial-owner details are filed by the company's own officer, so a provider files only if it is itself an officer. A company's CY Login profile is verified in person at a centre by an officer, or by a provider with his signed authorisation. Planning applications are made in the owner's name or by his authorised representative, through a designer he authorises. Biometrics need the person.

  10. The advocates' Pension Fund stamps reached filings at the Registrar of Companies only in 1988. As published on 15 September 1966 (K.D.P. 643/1966, under s. 27 of the Advocates Law), regulation 3 of the Fees Regulations charged an advocate's appearances before a court and the filing of listed documents with a court or court officer; the 1968 and 1976 amendments added no Registrar filings. K.D.P. 103/1988 (Gazette of 26 March 1988) inserted regulation 3(3) and replaced the Table with one whose new Part III covered filings with the Official Receiver and Registrar of Companies and the Ship Registrar; its first item was the application to register a business name, then £1.

No general Cyprus statute on how a power of attorney is executed was found on 6 October 2026: cylaw's index of Chapters has none, and the Contract Law (Cap. 149, Part XIII 'Agency') says only that authority may be express or implied, express when given orally or in writing (ss. 146-147). Specific acts set formalities: for a land transfer or mortgage through an agent, Law 9/1965 s. 10 requires a written authority certified by a certifying officer (or mukhtar) if signed in Cyprus, or by a Cyprus consular officer if signed abroad. Under K.D.P. 48/2024, private documents for use abroad, such as powers of attorney, go on to the Justice Ministry or citizen service centres.

A Cyprus advocate's annual practising licence is issued or renewed only if he holds professional-negligence insurance with a licensed insurer (Advocates Law, Cap. 2, s. 6E(1)); the Bar Council fixes the minimum cover (s. 6E(2)). The Council's decision on basic specifications, the document the Bar links on 6 October 2026 (file created 25 March 2013), sets minimum limits of €170,860 per claim and €341,720 per insurance period, plus at least €25,630 for defence costs, a deductible of at most 1% of the limit per claim, and cover for practice in the EEA on the basis of Cyprus law; the insured include the lawyer's LLC, employees and his own service, management or trustee companies.

  21. A client unhappy with a Cyprus lawyer has two routes on the Bar's pages (read 6 October 2026). Conduct: a written complaint to the Advocates' Disciplinary Board, a statutory body chaired by the Attorney General, with a €68 fee, for fraudulent, disgraceful or unprofessional conduct or breach of the conduct rules; mishandling a case is not itself an offence. A private complaint proceeds only with the Board's leave, and if the advocate is acquitted the complainant may be ordered to pay costs (Cap. 2, s. 17(2), (3)(δ)). Fees in a non-court matter: a Bar committee of three advocates under K.D.P. 171/2018, whose decisions have the status of arbitral awards enforceable through a District Court.

Under Cyprus's Advocates Law (Cap. 2, s. 17, cylaw text through Law 17(I)/2024, read 6 October 2026) the Disciplinary Board may warn or reprimand an advocate, fine him up to €20,000, suspend his licence or strike him off. A person complaining of an advocate's conduct starts proceedings only with the Board's leave (s. 17(3)(δ)), and if the advocate is acquitted the Board may order the complainant to pay the costs, assessed on the €10,000-€50,000 scale of civil actions (s. 17(2)). The Bar's public page 'Inadequate Professional Services', read the same day, still gives the fine limit as one thousand pounds.

  24. Cyprus lawyers have had no minimum fees for out-of-court work since 29 June 2018, when K.D.P. 172/2018 repealed the minimum-fee regulations of 1985-2017 and K.D.P. 171/2018 took effect. Under the latter an advocate must tell the client in advance how the fee will be set, 'especially' when it is hourly, and must deliver a fee account within a reasonable time and at the latest one month after the client asks; breach is a disciplinary offence (regs 7-9). The conduct rules (K.D.P. 237/2002, reg 19 as replaced by K.D.P. 142/2013) let an advocate inform the public about his services in any medium if the information is accurate and not misleading; they say nothing specific on publishing prices.

  7. For a company, limited liability in Cyprus comes from incorporation under the Companies Law, Cap. 113: under s. 3(1) seven or more persons, or for a private company 'one or more persons', associated for any lawful purpose may form a company with limited liability by subscribing the memorandum and registering; under s. 3(2)(α) each member of a company limited by shares is liable only for any amount unpaid on his shares. A one-person private company is therefore possible. A limited partner is not liable beyond his contribution, but a limited partnership needs at least one general partner liable for all its debts (Cap. 116, s. 47(2)). Read 6 October 2026.

  8. Public tenders in Cyprus are not reserved to companies. The Public Procurement Law 73(I)/2016 defines an 'economic operator' as any natural or legal person, public body or group of them that offers works, products or services on the market (s. 2), and s. 45(1) forbids rejecting operators entitled to provide a service in their home member state 'solely on the ground' that Cyprus law would require them to be natural or legal persons; groups may bid without a particular legal form, which may be required only after award (s. 45(3)-(4)). Read 6 October 2026, consolidated text with amendments through Law 113(I)/2025.

  13. What a Cyprus partnership owes each year. It keeps books (Cap. 116, s. 64). Only where the sole or all general partners are limited companies (Cypriot, EU or comparable) or partnerships do the Companies Law's annual-return and accounts rules apply: the return within six months of the year-end, a late one charged €50, €1 a day for six months and €2 a day after, up to €500 (s. 64A). For tax, every partnership with business income has its accounts audited or reviewed by a licensed auditor unless the Commissioner exempts it (Law 4/1978, s. 30(1)(b): 'person' includes a partnership, which lacks the individual's turnover exemption). It is not a 'company' for income tax (Law 118(I)/2002, s. 2).

  16. A partnership carrying on business in Cyprus, general or limited, must register with the Registrar of Companies within one month of its formation (Cap. 116, ss. 50(α), 51(1)). The statement, signed by all partners, gives the firm name, the nature and principal place of business, each partner's name, nationality and usual residence (for a legal person its name and office), the term and start date, whether it is a limited partnership, each limited partner's contribution, and the general partners authorised to manage and sign. Per the Registrar (read 5 October 2026): name approval first, then e-filing or form Σ1; fee €120, plus €40 accelerated; 'up to 100 partners'.

Liability in a Cyprus partnership (Cap. 116, read 5 October 2026): every partner in a firm is liable jointly with the other partners for all debts and obligations of the firm incurred while he is a partner (s. 12). A limited partnership has one or more general partners liable for all debts and one or more limited partners liable only up to the amount contributed (s. 47(2)); a legal person may be a limited partner (s. 47(4)); limited partnerships 'are not considered legal persons with separate legal personality' (s. 47(6)); and one that is not registered as such is deemed a general partnership, every limited partner a general partner (s. 48).

  18. A Cyprus business name carries no annual return and no yearly fee at the Registrar; Cap. 116 leaves four standing duties. Any change of the registered particulars is notified within seven days (s. 54(1)); cessation of business within one month (s. 57(1)); catalogues, circulars and business letters show the owner's name and, if he is not Cypriot, his nationality (s. 65(1)(β)); the Registrar may ask for the data to be confirmed (s. 58A(3)). A late notice of a new place of business or changed owner's particulars is charged up to €50 plus €1 a day, at most €250 (s. 61A(1)); while in default the owner cannot enforce the business's contracts by action unless a court grants relief (s. 62).

  22. A Cyprus business-name statement (Cap. 116, s. 52(1)) gives the name, nature and principal place of the business, its start date and, for an individual owner, names, nationality and usual residence. Cap. 116 sets no nationality or residence condition; the duty to register falls on a person with 'a place of business in Cyprus' trading under a name other than his surname with his forenames or initials (s. 50(β)). Per the Registrar (read 6 October 2026) the name is approved first (€10 per name, €20 more accelerated; reserved six months), then filed within a month of starting business, by e-filing with a solemn declaration of the signatures' witness or on form EE1: €80, €40 more accelerated.

  25. Limited liability in a Cyprus company has a statutory exception applied by the court in a winding up. Under s. 311(1) of the Companies Law, Cap. 113, if in a winding up it appears that any business of the company was carried on with intent to defraud creditors of the company or of any other person, or for any fraudulent purpose, the Court, on application of the Official Receiver, the liquidator or any creditor or contributory, may, if it thinks proper, declare persons knowingly party to it personally responsible, 'without any limitation of liability', for all or any of the company's debts or liabilities as it directs; s. 311(3) also makes this an offence. Read 6 October 2026.

  2. The thresholds Mastercard still prints are MATCH Pro listing reasons (Security Rules and Procedures - Merchant Edition, 4 August 2026). Code 04 'Excessive Chargebacks': the merchant's Mastercard chargebacks over the previous three months exceeded 1.5% of its sales transactions and reached USD 5,000 in total. Code 05 'Excessive Fraud': a fraud-to-sales dollar ratio of 8% or greater and 10 or more fraudulent transactions 'equal to or greater than USD 5,000' in the previous three months. Up to the edition of 6 August 2024 both were measured in one month: code 04 at 1%, code 05 with fraud 'totaling USD 5,000 or more'. The three-month wording first appears in the 11 February 2025 edition.

  3. The PCI Security Standards Council is closing its two older phone-acceptance standards. A bulletin of 1 May 2026 opened a formal sunset period for PCI SPoC (Software-based PIN Entry on COTS) and PCI CPoC (Contactless Payments on COTS) running from 1 May to 31 October 2026: new submissions are accepted during the period and none after it. Existing SPoC and CPoC listings stay valid through their normal lifecycle and expire on their existing re-evaluation or expiry dates. The Council gives the continued expansion and maturity of MPoC as the reason and points vendors to MPoC 'where appropriate'. As of 4 October 2026 the sunset period is still running.

Visa's public VAMP fact sheet (unchanged since at least 15 July 2025; read 5 October 2026) defines the VAMP ratio, for card-not-present transactions, as the count of fraud reports (TC40) plus disputes (TC15) divided by the count of settled transactions (TC05). An acquirer is 'Above Standard' at 50 basis points or more and 'Excessive' at 70 or more; a merchant of an acquirer that is neither is 'Excessive' at 220 or more, which the sheet says is cut to 150 on 1 April 2026 (AP, Canada, EU, US). Each level also requires at least 1,500 fraud-plus-dispute items a month there. Two enumeration thresholds are listed: a ratio of 2,000 basis points or more and 300,000 or more enumerated authorisations.

No PCI DSS self-assessment questionnaire is written for reader-less tap-on-phone acceptance: on 2 October 2026 the Council's Document Library listed nine merchant questionnaires, none for CPoC or MPoC solutions. SAQ SPoC, new with PCI DSS v4.0 (September 2023), is only for attended card-present merchants that enter all card data through a PCI-listed secure card reader (SCRP) paired with a phone or tablet in a listed solution.   9. PCI DSS v4.0 added 64 new requirements (the Council's total): 13 applied at once to all v4.0 assessments, 51 were best practice until 31 March 2025, then mandatory. Of the 51, 41 are marked for all entities and 10 for service providers only (our count). The all-entity ones include 6.4.3 and 11.6.1 (payment-page scripts, tamper detection), 6.4.2 (automated protection of public web applications), 8.3.6 (passwords of 12 characters, or 8 where the system cannot support 12), 8.4.2 (multi-factor authentication for all access into the cardholder data environment), 5.4.1, 11.3.1.2 and 12.3.1. A merchant's questionnaire decides which apply: SAQ A dropped 6.4.3, 11.6.1 and 12.3.1 in January 2025.

The PCI standard for card acceptance on a phone is Mobile Payments on COTS (MPoC): published on 16 November 2022, revised as v1.0.1 in February 2023 and v1.1 in November 2024, still current in the Council's Document Library on 2 October 2026. MPoC builds on the two older standards - Software-based PIN Entry on COTS (SPoC) and Contactless Payments on COTS (CPoC) - allowing PIN and contactless entry on the same off-the-shelf device, with three product types: MPoC Software, an Attestation and Monitoring Service, an MPoC Solution. They are evaluated by PCI-recognised laboratories; the Council 'encourages' merchants and acquirers to choose a listed one and leaves any mandate to the brands.

PCI DSS v4.0.1 has nine merchant self-assessment questionnaires (SAQ Instructions and Guidelines, v4.0.1 r1, April 2025): A - card-not-present merchants outsourcing all account data functions; A-EP - e-commerce sites that do not receive card data but affect the payment page's security; B - imprint or dial-out terminals; B-IP - standalone PCI-approved terminals with an IP connection; C-VT - manual entry into a third-party virtual terminal; C - payment applications connected to the internet; P2PE - terminals in a PCI-listed point-to-point encryption solution; SPoC - a phone or tablet with a listed secure card reader; D - all other merchants. All but D assume no electronic card-data storage.

Visa dispute time limits (Visa Core Rules, edition 18 April 2026): an issuer may dispute fraud in a card-absent transaction (condition 10.4) within 120 calendar days of the transaction processing date, and a declined-authorisation case (11.2) within 75. For merchandise or services not received (13.1) the limit is 120 days from the processing date or from the last date the cardholder expected delivery, not beyond 540 days from the processing date, after a 15-day wait in listed cases. The acquirer then has 30 calendar days from the dispute processing date: a pre-arbitration attempt for fraud and authorisation disputes, a dispute response for processing-error and consumer disputes.

Visa's public rules (edition 18 April 2026) put wallets that hand the card credential to the merchant - the model of Apple Pay and Google Pay - in their own class, 'Pass-Through Digital Wallet', outside the 'Digital Wallet Operator' class. The glossary defines it as functionality of a non-issuer that is usable at more than one merchant, stores a payment credential and transfers it directly to the merchant, after which the merchant 'finalizes the Transaction with its Acquirer, and the Pass-Through Digital Wallet is not involved in the Authorization, Clearing, or Settlement payment flow'. A Digital Wallet Operator is one operating a staged or stored-value wallet. Visa names no wallet brand.

A 'Pass-through Digital Wallet' is functionality by which the operator stores account data provided by the cardholder and, at a transaction, 'transfers the Account data to the Merchant or Sponsored Merchant or to its Acquirer or the Acquirer's Service Provider'; its operator is 'a Digital Activity Customer or other Customer, approved by the Corporation'. Rule 9.2.2 forbids a pass-through operator to charge a merchant 'any fee or other charge for the acceptance of Mastercard Account credentials' (other fees only by agreement) or to restrict which interfaces a merchant supports.

  20. Cyprus statutory periods counted in days exclude the starting day: s. 31(α) of the Interpretation Law, Cap. 1 (cylaw consolidated text read 5 Oct 2026) says that, in computing time for the purposes of a Law or public instrument and unless the contrary appears, a period of days from an event is deemed to exclude the day on which the event happens; under s. 31(β), if the last day is a Sunday or public holiday the period includes the next day that is neither. Saturdays are not named. By its terms this governs the 60 days for a company's Tax Register notice and the 90 days for its first beneficial-owner filing, both counted from incorporation.

  14. Money held with a Cyprus electronic money or payment institution is safeguarded, not deposit-guaranteed. By statute it is not a deposit (Electronic Money Law 81(I)/2012 art. 15(3)-(4); Payment Services Law 31(I)/2018 art. 18(3)), and recital 29 of Directive 2014/49/EU keeps e-money outside deposit guarantee. Law 31(I)/2018 art. 10(1), replaced by Law 100(I)/2025 (June 2025) and now covering EMIs, gives two methods: no commingling and, by the end of the next day, a separate account at a credit institution or central bank, or secure low-risk assets; or insurance or a comparable guarantee from an insurer or credit institution outside the group. Scheme members are credit institutions only.

Non-bank access to central-bank payment rails in Cyprus: the TARGET-CY System (Amending) Directive of 2025, K.D.P. 293/2025 (Official Gazette Annex III(I) No. 5972, 3 October 2025), in force from 6 October 2025, adds 'non-bank payment service providers' as defined in ECB Decision (EU) 2025/222 — payment institutions and e-money institutions — to the entities the Central Bank of Cyprus 'may at its discretion' admit as TARGET-CY participants.   1. From 10 July 2027 Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (AMLR; in force, applies then) adds two foreign-element duties. Nominee shareholders and directors must disclose their status, nominator and its beneficial owners to the legal entity, which reports them to the central register and to obliged entities (art. 66). A legal entity created outside the Union must first file its beneficial owners with the register of the Member State where it buys real estate or costly vehicles, vessels or aircraft, wins a public contract, or opens a business relationship with an obliged entity - the last only if that obliged entity, or the foreign entity's type or sector, is rated medium-high or high risk (art. 67).

  2. Unlike the companies register, Cyprus's register of beneficial owners of trusts (kept by CySEC under s. 61Γ of the AML Law) has a published legitimate-interest route. Under CySEC Directive K.D.P. 257/2021 as amended by K.D.P. 77/2025 (in force 18 March 2025), a person files a duly substantiated request to CySEC through the register's system (para. 13) and pays €75 per express trust or similar arrangement for a written report (para. 10(4)); obliged entities pay €4 per trust (para. 10(3)). K.D.P. 243/2026 (Gazette No. 6026, 29.5.2026, in force on publication) deleted only para. 14 and fee para. 10(5) - the route of s. 61Γ(12)(δ), which Law 25(I)/2026 art. 4(γ) had removed. Read 5 Oct 2026.

  3. For the beneficial-owner register the Cyprus Registrar of Companies offers access through CY Login by the legal entity's own profile or by that of its official (a natural or legal person). Its guidance page (served 5 October 2026) marks the official route: 'Currently this procedure applies only to Cypriot citizens holding a Cypriot identity card'; its Guidance to the register, version 2.1 of February 2025, repeats this and adds that identification 'via passport number is not accepted'. On these texts a non-Cypriot director files through the company's own profile. CY Login's help page, the same day, accepts residence permits and EU registration certificates for natural-person profiles.

The central register of beneficial owners of companies and other legal entities in Cyprus is drawn up, kept and published by the Registrar of Companies under s. 61A(4)(β) of the AML Law (Law 188(I)/2007). Its rules are in the Registrar's Directive K.D.P. 112/2021 (Official Gazette No. 5479, 12.3.2021), amended by K.D.P. 317/2021, 101/2022, 116/2022, 401/2023, 34/2024, 120/2024 and 423/2024; no later amendment appears in the cylaw index of regulatory acts to 25 Sep 2026. Filing through an interim system opened on 16 March 2021 and the final system went live on 14 November 2023. The register is electronic only; no documents or fees are submitted when filing.

  19. Cyprus banks must report beneficial-ownership discrepancies. Art. 61A(5)(b) of Law 188(I)/2007 obliges obliged entities to report to the Registrar of Companies any difference they find between the beneficial-owner information in the register and the information available to them, and CBC Directive of 2025 para 37(13) requires the bank to investigate such a difference and, where necessary, file a suspicion report with MOKAS. According to the Registrar, discrepancy reports can be submitted electronically since 1 April 2024, and the company is given 30 days to answer the Registrar's notice with a reasoned statement and evidence. In force on 4 October 2026.

  1. Law 36(I)/2023 (Official Gazette No. 4947, 2 June 2023) amended Article 60(1) of the Cyprus Payment Services Law 31(I)/2018 by replacing its opening word 'Where' with 'Subject to paragraph (5) of Article 62, where'. Since then the duty to tell the payer in advance about a charge or discount for a given payment instrument is expressly subordinate to the rule that a payee may not request charges for using a specific payment instrument. The preamble says the Law re-harmonises with Article 60(1) of Directive (EU) 2015/2366; PSD2 Article 62(5) lets Member States 'prohibit or limit the right of the payee to request charges'. CyLaw's consolidated text, read 4 October 2026, shows the new wording.

  2. The Cyprus Government reads Article 62(5) of Law 31(I)/2018 as a ban with no exceptions. The report of the House Finance and Budget Committee of 23 May 2023 records the Ministry of Finance explaining that the Consumer Protection Service, investigating complaints about payees charging for card use, had found an 'interpretative conflict' between Articles 60(1) and 62(5), and that 'the legislator's intention was the universal prohibition, without exceptions' of such charges. The Committee reserved its position for the plenary; the House then passed the Bill as Law 36(I)/2023. That commercial and three-party cards are covered is an inference from 'without exceptions', not the report's words.

  3. The Consumer Protection Service polices the Cyprus surcharge ban under powers written into the Payment Services Law by Law 16(I)/2022 (Official Gazette No. 4876, 4 March 2022). Article 99(1A) makes it the competent authority for payees' compliance with Articles 60 and 62; Article 99A lets it demand information from a payee, inspect its premises and order it to stop an infringement at once; Article 99B allows, after hearing the payee, an administrative fine of up to EUR 2,000 and, if the infringement continues, up to EUR 100 a day, recoverable as a civil debt. Giving the Service false information is a criminal offence (up to six months in prison, a fine up to EUR 10,000, or both).

Before a user is bound by a framework contract, Cyprus Law 31(I)/2018 art. 51(1) requires the provider to give, in good time and on paper or another durable medium, the terms listed in art. 52, in clear wording and in an official language of the Member State of the service or another agreed one; a draft contract suffices (art. 51(3)). Art. 52 lists seven groups: the provider, use of the service, charges and rates, communication, safeguards and liability, changes and termination, and redress including any choice of law or court. Art. 53 lets the user obtain the terms on request at any time; art. 40(1) bars charging for it; art. 41 makes the provider prove it met these information duties.

Unauthorised payments under Cyprus Law 31(I)/2018 (read 4 Oct 2026): the user notifies without undue delay and within 13 months of the debit date (art. 71(1)); the provider must prove authentication and accurate recording, and recorded use of an instrument is not necessarily sufficient proof of authorisation (art. 72); the provider refunds by the end of the next business day unless it has reasonable grounds to suspect fraud and reports them to the Central Bank in writing (art. 73(1)); the payer may bear up to EUR 50 for a lost, stolen or misappropriated instrument - nothing if it was undetectable to him beforehand - and all losses if he acted fraudulently or with gross negligence (art. 74).

  9. A Cyprus merchant may not surcharge card payments. Article 62(4) of Law 31(I)/2018 repeats PSD2 Article 62(4): no charge for instruments with interchange regulated by Regulation (EU) 2015/751 or for payments under Regulation (EU) No 260/2012. Article 62(5), unchanged since 18 April 2018, adds, unqualified, that the payee is not permitted to request charges for the use of a specific payment instrument - on its wording also commercial and three-party cards. Paragraph (3) reproduces PSD2's cost-based allowance, and no court or Central Bank reading was found (4 October 2026). Visa section 1.5.5.2 (ID# 0006948, 18 April 2026) bans surcharges unless law expressly requires that they be permitted.

  10. The European Banking Authority does not license or supervise individual Cyprus payment firms. Under art. 15 of Directive (EU) 2015/2366 (PSD2; in force and not repealed per its CELLAR notice on 4 October 2026) it develops, operates and maintains the electronic central register of the information notified by national competent authorities (for Cyprus, the Central Bank), is responsible for presenting it accurately and makes it public free of charge; the national authorities remain responsible for the accuracy of what they notify and for keeping it up to date (art. 15(3)). EBA drafts the technical standards for the register, which the Commission adopts (art. 15(4)–(5)).

Changes to a framework contract under Cyprus Law 31(I)/2018 art. 54: the provider must propose any change to the contract or to the art. 52 information at least two months before its proposed date of application, on paper or another durable medium (art. 54(1)); if the contract so provides, silence counts as acceptance, and the user may terminate free of charge before that date (art. 54(2)). Changes in interest or exchange rates may apply immediately and without notice if the contract says so and they follow agreed reference rates (art. 54(3)); rate changes in the user's favour need no notice (proviso to art. 54(4)). Charges are art. 52 information, so a fee change falls under art. 54(1).

Ending a framework contract under Cyprus Law 31(I)/2018 art. 55: the user may terminate at any time unless a notice period of not more than one month is agreed (art. 55(1)); termination is free of charge unless the contract has been in force for less than six months, and any charge must be reasonable and in line with costs (art. 55(2)); the provider may terminate a contract of indefinite duration only if the contract so provides and with at least two months' notice on paper or another durable medium (art. 55(3)); regular charges are due only pro rata and prepaid charges are refunded pro rata (art. 55(4)). Art. 55(5) leaves national rules on rescission and nullity untouched.

What the PSD2 transposition changed in the statutory terms of a framework contract in Cyprus: the repealed Payment Services Law 128(I)/2009 let a user terminate free of charge only after 12 months from conclusion (art. 43(2)) and capped the payer's liability for a lost or stolen instrument at EUR 150 (art. 57(2)); Law 31(I)/2018, in force from 18 April 2018, cut these to 6 months (art. 55(2)) and EUR 50 (art. 74(1)). Unchanged: two months' notice of contract changes (art. 42(1) of 2009; art. 54(1) of 2018), two months' notice of termination by the provider (art. 43(3); art. 55(3)), and a user notice period of not more than one month. Both laws treat micro-enterprises like consumers.

In its non-binding Opinion of 19 June 2020, C(2020) 4117 final, the Commission takes the view that once a listed person is determined to control an unlisted entity, control 'can be presumed' to extend to all its assets, which 'must be frozen' unless the entity shows, under national procedure, that given assets are not controlled; funds made available to such an entity are 'in principle' made indirectly available to the listed person unless it is reasonably determined they will not reach him.

  1. Whether a newly formed Cyprus company may have a review instead of an audit in its first or second financial year is not answered by any public official text found as of 4 Oct 2026. Section 152A(1)(d) of the Companies Law requires the limits to be met for at least two consecutive financial years; ICPAC's TC 2/2026 (19 February 2026) repeats this, has no first-period example and refers to TC 5/2022 'Guide to Review Engagements' (10 August 2022), whose link leads to the members' login. The Registrar's news list has six items for 2026 to 30 September, none on it. Tax Department guidance was not searched. The one explicit statement found is a provider's: the first two periods need an audit.

ICPAC's Technical Circular 2/2026 (19 February 2026, Audit and Assurance Committee) reads the commencement of art. 5 of Law 2(I)/2026 as follows: because art. 5 entered into force on publication, the €300,000 net-turnover limit for choosing a review instead of an audit applies to reporting periods beginning on or after 6 February 2026; periods beginning earlier are tested against €200,000. For a calendar-year company the first financial year under the new limit is therefore 2027, not 2026. The Law itself has no transitional clause: art. 7(2) only says art. 5 enters into force on publication. This is the professional body's reading, not a ruling of the Registrar or a court.

Cyprus tax law does not narrow the review option for companies: s. 30(1)(b) of Law 4/1978 requires accounts that are 'audited or reviewed ... as provided in the Companies Law' by a person licensed to be appointed company auditor, and s. 5(1A) ties the later return deadline to accounts that are 'audited or reviewed'. Section 29, as replaced by Law 243(I)/2025 (in force 1 January 2026), lets the tax authority disregard accounts not prepared and certified by a statutory auditor or audit firm, and tax computations not prepared and certified by a holder of a practising certificate from ICPAC or another recognised body of auditors. Read on cylaw 4 Oct 2026.

Under s. 142(2)(a) of the Cyprus Companies Law (Cap. 113) a company's financial statements are filed with the Registrar no later than 18 months after incorporation, then at least once every calendar year, and within 12 months of the balance-sheet date (the 12-month limit was added by Law 191(I)/2020, Gazette No. 4794, 17.12.2020). The Registrar's guidance, read 4 Oct 2026, adds that none are filed in the year of incorporation, nor in the next year if a general meeting was held in the year of incorporation. Under s. 151(1)(η)-(θ) unlisted small-sized companies are exempt from the management report; medium-sized ones only from its non-financial information; the guidance wrongly exempts both.

  1. The Central Bank of Cyprus publishes its own English texts of the deposit-guarantee rules: an unofficial consolidation of the Scheme Regulations of 2016 to (No. 2) of 2020 (latest update 16 November 2020) and of the Scheme Laws of 2016 to 2021 (latest update 30 July 2021). Its 'Legal Framework DGS' page, as served on 5 October 2026, lists the basic Regulations and four amendments (2016, 2018, 2020 and No. 2 of 2020) and the basic Law and four amendments (2018, two of 2020, 2021), and nothing later. The consolidation gives the look-through rule as reg. 10(e), the client-account holder's information duty as reg. 10(g) and the e-money exclusion as s. 3(2) of the Law.

Reg. 8(2) of K.D.P. 27/2016 covered such deposits - for example proceeds of transactions in private residential property - up to EUR 50,000 above the EUR 100,000 limit for up to six months; K.D.P. 84/2020 (6 March 2020), reg. 7(b), replaced 'fifty thousand euro (EUR 50,000)' with 'three hundred thousand euro (EUR 300,000)' and 'six (6)' with 'twelve (12)'. EBA Opinion EBA/Op/2021/11 of 27 October 2021 found that deposit guarantee schemes treated client funds differently as Member States read arts. 5(1) and 7(3) of Directive 2014/49/EU differently: among the 27 of 30 EEA states that answered its survey, client funds placed with banks by payment institutions were covered in 16 and not in 10 (one unsure), those placed by e-money institutions in 13 and not in 13 (one unsure).   4. The term 'client account' entered Cyprus's deposit-guarantee regulations with K.D.P. 84/2020 (6 March 2020): an account whose absolute beneficiaries are persons other than those in whose name it is held and which is held on their behalf. The same instrument added reg. 10(g): every holder of a client account must obtain and keep accurate and up-to-date information on the persons absolutely entitled to the money, including their identity, and give it to the credit institution and/or the scheme's Management Committee within seven working days of a request. The definition does not depend on who the holder is and mentions neither payment or e-money institutions nor safeguarding.

  5. Deposits with credit institutions established in Cyprus are covered by the Deposit Guarantee and Resolution of Credit and Other Institutions Scheme up to EUR 100,000 per depositor per credit institution, including accrued interest (CBC page and FAQ, read 4 October 2026). Company deposits are eligible, but 'deposits by financial institutions' are excluded; it is the CBC's FAQ, not the regulation text read, that counts as such companies whose main activity is acquiring participations (holding companies), lending, leasing, payment services or portfolio management. The EU definition behind the exclusion (CRR art. 4(1)(26), as amended in 2024) carves out a 'pure industrial holding company'.

  6. Directive (EU) 2026/804 of 30 March 2026 (OJ 20 April 2026, in force 10 May 2026) amends the Deposit Guarantee Schemes Directive to cover safeguarding accounts expressly. A new art. 8b obliges Member States to guarantee 'client funds deposits' that financial institutions place with a bank for the account of their clients, where the clients are themselves eligible, the deposits sit in segregated accounts under EU safeguarding rules, and the clients are identified or identifiable. The EUR 100,000 limit applies to each client and, by derogation from art. 7(1), the client's own deposits at the same bank are not added. Member States must adopt the measures by, and apply them from, 11 May 2028.

  7. Does Cyprus's deposit guarantee cover customers of a payment or e-money institution whose safeguarding account is at a Cyprus bank? On 4 October 2026 the texts pull two ways. The regulations define a 'client account' regardless of who holds it and cover the persons absolutely entitled (K.D.P. 27/2016 reg. 10(e), K.D.P. 84/2020); 'irrespective of the account holder' is FAQ wording only. That fits a payment institution's segregated account. But art. 3(2) of Law 5(I)/2016 puts 'amounts defined as electronic money' outside the scheme, which tells against cover for e-money holders. No Cyprus text names safeguarding accounts; the express EU rule (Directive (EU) 2026/804) applies from 11 May 2028.

The Central Bank of Cyprus' deposit-guarantee FAQ (file dated 8 October 2025, q.24) states that, irrespective of the account holder, the scheme covers the absolute beneficiaries of 'client accounts', provided they are not themselves in an excluded category, and that the holder must keep up-to-date information on them. Deposits held by payment service providers in their own right fall under the excluded 'deposits by financial institutions' (FAQ q.15(d)).   9. The look-through rule of Cyprus's deposit guarantee scheme is reg. 10(e) of the Deposit Guarantee and Resolution of Credit and Other Institutions Scheme Regulations (K.D.P. 27/2016, 11 February 2016): where the depositor is not absolutely entitled to the sums in an account, the guarantee covers the person who is, provided that person's identity is or can be established before the deposit becomes unavailable; where several are entitled, each one's share under the arrangements governing the money counts towards the EUR 100,000 limit. The Regulations were amended by K.D.P. 73/2016, 136/2018, 84/2020 and 267/2020; the CyLaw lists for 2021-2026 show no later amendment (checked 4 October 2026).

  10. Cyprus's deposit-guarantee statute excludes electronic money in terms. Art. 3(2) of the Deposit Guarantee and Resolution of Credit and Other Institutions Scheme Law 5(I)/2016 (CyLaw consolidated text with amendments up to Law 119(I)/2021, read 4 October 2026) provides that amounts defined as electronic money under the Electronic Money Law do not fall within the scope of the Law; art. 3(1) applies the Law to credit institutions. The Law itself contains no rule on client or beneficiary accounts - the words for 'client account', 'absolutely entitled' and 'beneficiary' do not occur in it; those rules sit in the Regulations made under its art. 32 (K.D.P. 27/2016 as amended).

  1. A natural person - a sole trader - may register in Cyprus as an employer. The Social Insurance Services' form YKA 1-001 (edition 9/2021, linked on their employer-registration page updated 30 September 2026; read 6 October 2026) has a block 'to be completed only if the employer is a natural person' (date he became an employer, kind of business, activity, NACE code) beside one for a legal person, partnership or other entity, and asks for the employer's surname, nationality, social insurance number and identity card, EU registration, alien registration or passport number. Its document list names items only for companies and partnerships, not for a natural person.

  2. Cyprus's minimum wage is reviewed on a fixed cycle. Para 7 of the Minimum Wage Decree 2022 (K.D.P. 350/2022) sets an adjustment mechanism: a nine-member committee reports to the Minister of Labour at least two months before each revision and the Minister proposes an adjustment - which may be zero - to the Council of Ministers; it applied first on 1 January 2024 and 'thereafter every two years'. The 2024 and 2026 rates followed that cycle (K.D.P. 402/2023, K.D.P. 427/2025), so the next revision falls on 1 January 2028. Paras 10-11 allow reductions: by agreement up to 15% where the employer provides food and up to 10% for accommodation; 25% for casual work of under-18s up to two months.

How an employer identifies the person in a hire notice in Cyprus's Ergani system depends on nationality, per the system's user manual (PDF of 7 September 2021, linked from the Ergani login page on 5 Oct 2026), s. 4.2.1. Cypriot: identity-card number or social insurance number. Citizen of an EU state: an EU identity number with the country, an alien registration number and/or a social insurance number; if the match fails, the notice can go on once an identification file is uploaded.   4. A Cyprus company owes a director a written statement of terms if he is its employee. Law 25(I)/2023 on Transparent and Predictable Working Conditions (transposing Directive (EU) 2019/1152) applies to 'all employees' except those working on average up to three hours a week; seafarers and fishermen are covered with carve-outs (art. 4). 'Employee' (art. 3) turns on an employment relationship, 'taking into account the case law of the Court of Justice'. The employer gives the basic terms (parties, place, job, start date, pay, working time and others) on paper or electronically within seven calendar days of the start, the rest within one month (arts 11-12). No exception for directors is named.

  7. Cyprus's Minimum Wage Decree has no exception and no rule for directors or shareholders. K.D.P. 350/2022 applies to 'all employees in the Republic' (para 3(1)); an employee is a person working for another under a contract or relationship of employment or apprenticeship, or in circumstances from which an employer-employee relationship can be inferred (para 2). Outside it (3(2)-(5)): domestic, farm and livestock workers, seafarers; workers under more favourable arrangements; hotel staff under their own decree; trainees for a diploma or profession. Article 10 of Regulation (EU) 2015/751, applicable from 9 June 2016, forbids schemes and payment service providers to oblige a merchant that accepts one issuer's card to accept all other cards of the same scheme; the exception is consumer cards of the same brand and same category (prepaid, debit or credit) subject to the interchange caps, and a merchant that does not accept all cards must say so at the shop entrance and at the till, or on its website. Scheme rules follow: a Visa 'Limited Acceptance Merchant' in the EEA that accepts credit cards must accept all EEA-issued credit cards but need not accept EEA-issued commercial cards (Visa section 1.5.4.6, ID# 0008680, edition 18 April 2026).

  1. With 3-D Secure, fraud liability moves to the issuer under both schemes. Visa's condition 10.4 (card-absent fraud; edition 18 April 2026) makes a dispute invalid for a transaction sent with Electronic Commerce Indicator 5 where the issuer confirmed authentication using Visa Secure with EMV 3DS and the CAVV was in the authorisation request, and for ECI 6 with an attempt response and a CAVV, unless the card is a non-reloadable prepaid card. Mastercard's Chargeback Guide (19 May 2026) lists as ineligible for the fraud chargeback 4837 'properly authenticated transactions' with security level indicators 211, 212, 217 or 242, naming Identity Check as an example. Other grounds stay available.

The vendor Netcetera announced on 10 August 2022 that Mastercard would decommission it on 18 October 2022, and on 3 October 2023 in India and Bangladesh.

payfac 6

  1. Under Visa section 5.3.1.4 (ID# 0030891, edition 18 April 2026, last updated Oct 2025) an acquirer must sign a direct Merchant Agreement with a Sponsored Merchant that 'exceeds USD 1 million in annual Transaction volume' - before processing for a merchant new to the facilitator, or within 2 years after an existing one crosses it. 'Transaction' is a glossary term tied to Visa-branded Cards, so the base is the merchant's own Visa volume. Exempt: relationships held 2 years with the same acquirer, with reporting and continued acquirer oversight, and listed MCCs (utilities, healthcare, schools, tax and others). Brazil and Chile are carved out; there is no Europe variation.

  1. Law 41(I)/2026 (Official Gazette no. 5082, 2 April 2026), adopted 'for re-harmonisation with article 16 of Directive 2014/92/EU', replaced art. 17(9) of Cyprus Law 64(I)/2017: a bank may no longer refuse a payment account with basic features on the ground that the consumer already holds a payment account with another credit institution in Cyprus. It also deleted art. 17(10) (the bank's check for an existing account) and art. 20(2)(e) (termination because the consumer later opened a second account). Before the amendment the law allowed such a refusal. On 4 October 2026 CyLaw's consolidated text does not yet incorporate the change.

Bank of Cyprus' 'Payment Account with basic features' (read 4 October 2026) is addressed to physical persons legally residing in the European Union, is opened at a branch, is limited to one per customer, carries no overdraft or chequebook and can be linked only to a Classic Visa debit card; the page states 'The customer cannot be a legal entity'. The maximum charge is EUR 36 per calendar year provided the number of transactions does not exceed 100. For such applicants the CBC Directive of 2025 (para 32) accepts identification on official documents issued by the Cypriot authorities, such as the special residence permit or refugee travel document, and address verification by sworn affidavit.

  3. Cyprus transposed Directive 2014/92/EU by Law 64(I)/2017 (Gazette no. 4604, 16 June 2017; amended 2020, 2021, 2026). All credit institutions must offer basic payment accounts to consumers (art. 17(1)) unless the Central Bank exempts one on a reasoned application (art. 17(2)); consumers legally resident in the EU, including asylum seekers, have the right to open one (art. 17(4)); the bank must decide within ten business days of a complete application (art. 17(7)) and must refuse if opening would breach Law 188(I)/2007 (art. 17(8)); services are free or reasonably priced (art. 19(1)). 'Consumer' is a natural person acting outside trade or profession (art. 2); legal entities have no such right.

Directive 2014/92/EU (in force, unamended on 4 October 2026) gives the right to a basic payment account to 'consumers legally resident in the Union', including asylum seekers and persons with no fixed address (art. 16(2)). A consumer is a natural person acting outside trade, business, craft or profession (art. 2(1)), so companies and individuals acting in business have no such right. The account covers deposits, cash withdrawals, direct debits, card payments and credit transfers (art. 17(1)). The bank must open or refuse within 10 business days of a complete application and must refuse if opening would breach AML rules (art. 16(3)-(4)). Chapter IV applies from 18 September 2016.

eu-aml-package 4

  1. Direct supervision by the EU Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA) had not started on 4 October 2026. Under art. 13(4) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1620 (consolidated text of 10 November 2025) AMLA must commence the first selection of 'selected obliged entities' by 1 July 2027, conclude it within six months, publish the list without undue delay and begin direct supervision six months after publication, which puts the start in 2028; selection is repeated every three years. Selected entities are credit and financial institutions or groups whose residual risk profile is high (art. 13(1)); where none qualifies in a Member State, an additional selection is run there (art. 13(3)).

Directive (EU) 2024/1640 must be transposed by 10 July 2027, except art. 74 (access to beneficial-ownership information for persons with a legitimate interest) by 10 July 2025, arts. 11, 12, 13 and 15 (access to beneficial-ownership registers) by 10 July 2026, and art. 18 (single access point to real-estate information) by 10 July 2029 (art. 78(1)). Regulation (EU) 2024/1620 establishing the Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA) has applied since 1 July 2025, with some articles applying from 26 June 2024 and art. 103 from 31 December 2025 (art. 108). Cyprus implemented art. 74 by Law 25(I)/2026 of 20 March 2026.

  3. Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (the AML Regulation, OJ 19 June 2024) applies from 10 July 2027, and from 10 July 2029 for football agents and professional football clubs (art. 90); on 4 October 2026 it is in force, unamended and not yet applicable. Art. 52(1) sets the ownership test for a beneficial owner at direct or indirect ownership of '25 % or more' of shares, voting rights or other ownership interest, against '25% plus one share' or 'more than 25%' in art. 2 of Cyprus Law 188(I)/2007. For higher-risk categories of entities the Commission may set a lower threshold by delegated act: at most 15%, unless it finds a higher one more proportionate, in any case below 25% (art. 52(2)).

  4. From 10 July 2027 Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 fixes the minimum identification data EU-wide, except in lower-risk cases (art. 22(1)). Natural person: all names and surnames, place and full date of birth, nationalities, national identification number where applicable, usual place of residence and, where available, tax identification number. Legal entity: legal form and name, registered office and principal place of business, country of creation, legal representatives and, where available, registration number, tax identification number and LEI, plus nominee shareholders and directors. Updates: at least yearly for higher-risk customers, every five years for others (art. 26(2)).

cysec 2

  1. Cyprus Securities and Exchange Commission (CySEC), continued under Law 73(I)/2009 (set up by a 2001 law that it repealed) — what it supervises: investment firms under Law 87(I)/2017; administrative (trust and company) service providers under Law 196(I)/2012; collective investment schemes and their managers; crypto-asset service providers — for all of which it is the AML supervisor under art. 59(1)(β) of Law 188(I)/2007. Under MiCA, national-regime providers had to apply by 27 February 2026 and their transitional period ended on 1 July 2026. ESMA's table of 7 July 2026 lists CySEC and the Central Bank of Cyprus as Cyprus's MiCA competent authorities; the designating act is the ministerial notification K.D.P. 310/2024 of 13 September 2024 under art. 56A of Law 73(I)/2009.

  2. MiCA in Cyprus: Regulation (EU) 2023/1114 applies from 30 December 2024 (Titles III and IV from 30 June 2024). Cyprus kept the full 18-month transitional period of Art. 143(3) (ESMA list); CySEC's announcements rest on that article directly. On 17 October 2024 CySEC stopped accepting CASP registrations under national rules; providers registered before 30 December 2024 could continue until 1 July 2026 or until authorisation was granted or refused, and CySEC set 27 February 2026 as the deadline to apply. As of 2026-10-04 the period has ended: crypto-asset services in Cyprus need a MiCA authorisation (Art. 63) or, for already-licensed financial entities, an Art. 60 notification.

shell-companies 2

  1. The Central Bank of Cyprus sent credit institutions a circular letter on shell companies on 14 June 2018; its text was not found (CBC site, web archive, 4 October 2026), though the CBC's circular of 2 November 2018 cites it and revises its definition. A law-firm alert of 20 June 2018 describes the June letter as notice of an intention, 'not yet officially adopted', to make banks avoid starting or renewing relationships with non-listed entities that have no physical presence beyond a mailing address, no established economic activity, registration where audited accounts need not be filed, or tax residence in a 'tax haven' or nowhere, and as a request to review the client base and report.

The Central Bank of Cyprus stated on 16 November 2023 that, as a result of its targeted supervisory actions, credit institutions had from the end of 2018 until then terminated relationships with 42,728 shell companies and closed 125,782 bank accounts; that it had imposed fines relating to AML/CFT inspections in 13 cases since 2015; and that a recruitment drive begun in 2019 had raised the headcount of its AML/CFT department by 50% by 2022. The statement gives no method, period breakdown or definition for the two counts.
